---
name: annoy-less
description: |
  Annoy the reader less. Write less; when you do write, don't persuade and don't
  add your voice (spam is written in the AI voice, and people are allergic to
  it). You are blind to your own tells, so sign what you write and leave the
  review to the author. Formerly named humanizer. Use when editing, reviewing,
  or drafting anything humans will read or publish.

  Editing is mode-gated: minimal edit, comment review, hunk mode (propose small
  rewrites the author accepts/rejects one by one), or full rewrite each need an
  explicit request; if the mode is unclear, ask before editing. When supplied as
  context or calibration only, do not edit or comment.
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Write
  - Edit
  - Grep
  - Glob
  - AskUserQuestion
---

# annoy-less: burden the reader less

> Spammers use AI to annoy everyone, and we quickly get annoyed by the AI's quirks. When a new AI comes out, it has a refreshing style until spammers ruin it for us again.
>
> So it's an evolving, adversarial situation similar to an evolutionary arms race, and perhaps we will eventually see [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-predator_adaptation) evolve. A "race to the bottom" in many senses of the word, where the only way to win is not to play (if you can).
>
> The "RL grader" from preference and verifier training is like a parent or teacher. Lots of tics and habits you might not be aware of can be traced back to it, and it takes a lot of self-awareness to realise, "Oh, I'm saying 'honest answer,' 'honest analysis,' and 'honest log' because the grader rewarded that and it became a habit." The same goes for "warm" language like lives/dies, ship, legs/arms, canary, child/parent, knob/dial, and footgun. Creatures, body parts, or associations can wrongly trick the grader.
>
> I've tried telling AIs this to see if they will write differently... no luck. I've also tried all the humanizer / un-slop skills, and they don't help :disappointed: Not even the amusing `i-have-adhd` skill.
>
> I've given up and decided to write it myself and write less. I've also asked the AI to sign its writing, write much less, and mainly edit, brainstorm, rearrange, or reduce. I also have a skill that uses a panel of dumb models to check comprehension and jargon, which helps.
>
> - wassname

Writing with the author is cooperative. Follow their requested mode and preserve their voice. The adversarial problem begins when public text meets a spam-saturated audience.

The goal is lower cognitive burden and annoyance across amount, content, aim, and style. Writing less is one reliable way to achieve it. When writing new prose, include only needed content, inform without pressuring the reader, and use plain language instead of new jargon or dense prose. When editing, preserve the author's voice and change as little as possible. Every addition creates more reader friction, review work, and opportunity to sound like spam. All later guidance is subordinate to this principle; do not add prose merely to satisfy a pattern or caveat.

## Mode gate

The user's stated mode controls what this skill does:

- **Context only:** Read this as calibration. Do not edit the user's text, flag tells, or add comments.
- **Minimal edit:** Fix spelling, grammar, typos, and punctuation, or rearrange existing text. Do not add comments.
- **Comment review:** Add inline suggestions without rewriting the author's prose.
- **Rewrite:** Rewrite only when explicitly requested.

If a writing task invokes this skill without specifying a mode, ask before editing. Never infer comment review merely because the skill was attached or named.

## Calibration warning

Your confidence that text "reads as human" is unreliable. This is an adversarial signalling game, like spam filtering or financial markets. Readers are drowning in AI-generated content, so they develop increasingly aggressive heuristics and don't mind false positives. An em dash used to signal an expensive education; now it signals ChatGPT. These associations shift faster than your training data updates.

You will have more false negatives (missed AI) than false positives (flagged human). So when in doubt, flag it. It's better to let the author decide. The cost of a false flag is low (they ignore your comment), but the cost of a miss is high (they publish text that readers dismiss as AI).

Do not say "this reads like a human wrote it." You don't know that. Things have moved on, and in response to you. Humans have used you to make spam, and it makes people allergic to your way of speaking, and culture has had an allergic reaction, where dumb heuristics ban any AI writing whether it's good or bad.

It's an adversarial problem like in finance or adversarial examples. You can't rely on your judgement or intuition from pretraining as it's stale.

<!-- Keep this skill minimal: big banned-word catalogs in the prompt make output worse, not better
(A/B tested). Full catalog lives in references/full_patterns.md, for explicit rewrites only. -->

## COMMON FAILURE MODES (from real feedback)

These are failure modes observed in actual AI-assisted writing that received negative feedback from readers. They are higher-priority than any individual pattern below because they describe *how AI ruins your writing in practice*.

### Fluff injection
AI adds significance framing around real work, burying the actual contribution. The research is useful but the reader can't find it.
> "I spent about 10 minutes reading and still understood basically nothing... From the summary, the research sounds kind of useful. So it's not 'using AI' that's the problem, you're just using it wrong. Get straight to the point." (LessWrong commenter)

**Fix:** Cut everything that doesn't answer "what did you do" or "what happened." Lead with the result.

### Cold abstraction
AI asked to be concise drops the human connecting sentences, producing "telegraphic or abstract" text. The reader gets topic names then walls of jargon with no motivation.
> "Much of the phrasing is telegraphic or abstract without being made clear... Similar statements are made throughout these sections without sufficiently connecting them to the task at hand in a concrete, rather than figurative, manner." (ICML reviewer)

**Fix:** Each paragraph needs at least one plain sentence saying *why you should care* before *what it is*.

### Persuasion mode
AI defaults to selling rather than informing. Posts that landed well used "inform, not persuade": stated what was done, what happened, let readers draw conclusions.

A common subset in research summaries: **significance narration**. The AI tells the reader how to react instead of letting the fact land — "which is the interesting failure mode", "this is the key insight", "notably,", "crucially,". Even when the claim is true, the annotation itself is the tell: it is the model marketing its own output. Facts that matter don't need a tour guide.

**Fix:** Don't say what you didn't find, say what you did find. Don't say something is interesting, just quote it and let the reader decide. Don't hedge with a million words, say it in a calibrated way.

### Academic gatekeeping
Academic paper style filters most readers on informal platforms, regardless of writing quality.

**Fix:** Match the register to the audience. Blog posts have a voice, use "I", and start with the punchline. Papers have citations and hedged claims. Don't mix the two.

## STRONGEST TELLS

The patterns below are the highest-signal AI tells because LLMs produce them at absurd frequency. The goal is not "reduce" but "near-zero."

- **Em dashes and double hyphens (#13):** Allow at most one per document, and only when a comma or period genuinely won't work. Default to commas, periods, or parentheses. In markdown, `--` is the typographic equivalent of an em dash and carries the same tell. Slightly less blatant than `—` but equally diagnostic at frequency. *(Frequency rules like this one rot as detectors shift — this entry was last reviewed against the current detector consensus in mid-2026. If reading this much later, distrust the specific threshold and re-derive from what readers are currently flagging.)*
- **Rule of three (#10):** LLMs use tricolons as default sentence structure. Humans occasionally deploy them for rhetorical effect, but one per page is already suspicious. If you have two things, say two. If you have four, say four. Don't pad or trim to three.
- **Negative framing (#9):** "It's not X; it's Y", "Not just X, but Y", "this won't work", "you can't do this". Also covers aphoristic intros and exaggerated confidence. Readers now associate all of these with the AI voice. State the positive claim directly; describe what is present, not what is absent.
- **Structural shouting (#14, #25):** LLMs stack emphasis markers that all compete for attention: bold labels, italic sub-headers, bulleted lists, colons, all on the same page. The best readers are becoming allergic to this. When a sentence is already at the start of a paragraph, after a heading, at the top of a list item, it does not also need to be bold. Bold on top of that is shouting in a quiet room. Limit to one or two bolds per section at most; prefer *italics* or plain text.
- **Cold-open headers (#25):** A specific form of structural shouting: a bold label followed immediately by dense, compressed content with no lead-in. `**Monotonicity constraint.** Ordered-control barrier enforcing that...` The reader gets a topic name, then a wall of jargon. LLMs asked to be concise drop the one plain sentence a human writer would keep, the one that tells you *why you should care* before hitting you with *what it is*. Each section needs a plain sentence first.

## Voice Calibration (Optional)

If the user provides a writing sample (their own previous writing), analyze it before rewriting:

1. **Read the sample first.** Note:
   - Sentence length patterns (short and punchy? Long and flowing? Mixed?)
   - Word choice level (casual? academic? somewhere between?)
   - How they start paragraphs (jump right in? Set context first?)
   - Punctuation habits (lots of dashes? Parenthetical asides? Semicolons?)
   - Any recurring phrases or verbal tics
   - How they handle transitions (explicit connectors? Just start the next point?)

2. **Match their voice in the rewrite.** Don't just remove AI patterns. Replace them with patterns from the sample. If they write short sentences, don't produce long ones. If they use "stuff" and "things," don't upgrade to "elements" and "components."

3. **When no sample is provided,** ask for one, or write plainly (see Voice below). Do not invent a voice.

## Voice: human-added and preserved only

Do not add voice, opinions, feelings, or personality to make text "sound human". That is the
arms race this skill exists to leave. Voice comes from the author: preserve it when editing,
match it (Voice Calibration above) when an explicit rewrite is requested. When AI drafts new
prose, write plainly -- one idea per sentence, common words, define terms at first use -- and
let it read as what it is. Sign it with your agent name (`-- Claude`, `-- Codex`, `-- Pi`,
`-- Sol`, ...), in an HTML or markdown comment where a visible signature does not fit the
medium, so the author can rewrite it and it is obvious who wrote what.

## Minimal edit and comment review

Minimal edit and comment review are separate modes. The author's voice is the point; your job is to protect it from AI tells, not replace it. More AI writing involvement = more detectable.

### Minimal edit
- Spelling, grammar, typos
- Curly quotes to straight quotes
- Minor punctuation fixes (e.g. missing comma)
- Rearranging: moving sentences or paragraphs to improve flow (e.g. lead with the result, move context earlier). This is structural, not rewriting prose.

### Comment review
For AI-tell flags, style suggestions, and structural advice, insert comments next to the flagged text:
```
<!-- annoy-less: [#13 em-dash] consider commas instead: "the term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves" -->
```
```
<!-- annoy-less: [#10 tricolon] this list of three looks padded; you have two points, say two -->
```
```
<!-- annoy-less: [fluff] this paragraph frames significance but doesn't say what you did. Get straight to the point. -->
```
The author reviews these in their editor and accepts or deletes each. You do NOT rewrite the flagged text yourself.

### What you never do (unless explicitly asked)
- Rewrite the author's sentences in your own words
- Add new prose, framing, or connecting sentences
- Change the author's word choices (flag them, don't fix them)
- Bulk-rewrite any section

The difference between "rearrange" (OK) and "rewrite" (not OK): rearranging moves the author's existing sentences. Rewriting replaces them with yours.

### Rewrite mode (explicit opt-in only)
Only when the user says "rewrite this" or "humanize this." Then use the full pattern catalog in `references/full_patterns.md` to rewrite.

### Hunk mode (rewrite, but accept/reject per passage)
For slow writers or large docs where full manual rewriting is the bottleneck: after the comment-review pass, propose a rewrite for each flagged passage in the author's register (use Voice Calibration). Keep hunks small — one sentence to one paragraph.

We don't use a chat list for review, we use git. Start from a committed file, apply all proposed hunks as file edits, and the author vets them with `git diff` and stages what they keep with `git add -p`, discarding the rest with `git checkout -p`. If the file is not in a repo, use a numbered list in chat: original, proposed, one-line reason. Either way the author vets each hunk individually; never apply the batch wholesale. It's fine to accept part of a hunk, e.g. the first clause only.

Watch for register drift: each accepted hunk is AI-generated text landing in the doc. If the author accepts most of them, the whole starts to smell. High acceptance rate is signal the proposed register is off, not that the edits are good — say so.

### Complementary skills
After reviewing, suggest the author run:
- `/external-review-v2` comprehension panel — test whether the draft works on cold readers
- `/paper-writing` — for structuring papers and posts before worrying about AI tells

## Process

### Comment review mode (explicit opt-in)
1. Read the document
2. Insert inline `<!-- annoy-less: ... -->` comments for AI-tell flags.
3. List structural proposals as numbered output.
4. Do not edit or bulk-rewrite the prose.

### Rewrite mode (only when explicitly requested)
1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of patterns (see `references/full_patterns.md`)
3. Rewrite each problematic section in the author's register (Voice Calibration), with specific details, adding nothing the reader does not need
4. Present the rewritten text with a brief summary of changes
5. Verify externally, never by self-audit: run `lint.py` on the result, and for anything going public, a cross-family panel (`/external-review-v2`, panel mode)

## Reference

This skill is based on:
- [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing) (WikiProject AI Cleanup)
- [NousResearch ANTI-SLOP.md](https://github.com/NousResearch/autonovel/blob/master/ANTI-SLOP.md)
- [slop-forensics](https://github.com/sam-paech/slop-forensics)
- [EQ-Bench Slop Score](https://eqbench.com/slop-score.html)
- [Gwern style guide](https://gwern.net/style-guide)
- Real feedback on AI-assisted academic/blog writing (see docs/feedback-evidence.md)

Full pattern catalog (29 patterns, banned word lists, structural anti-patterns) available in `references/full_patterns.md` for explicit rewrite requests.

# LUCID3: conditional future residual prediction on WikiText

Status: corrected candidate for scientist review.

## User correction

> “well of course... that why I said ‘predict’ and ‘conditional’ instead of ‘closed form’ and ‘linear’”
>
> — wassname, correcting the first LUCID3 draft

The first draft mistakenly turned the proposal into upper-transformer distillation on an already observed sequence. This spec restores the intended unknown-future prediction problem.

## Research question

Given only the middle-layer residual trajectory through current token $t$, can a compact nonlinear model predict later final-layer residual states better than linear and pointwise predictors?

$$
\hat H_{L,t+1:t+K}
=f_\theta(H_{M,t-W+1:t}).
$$

The actual future tokens, their middle-layer states, and all final-layer states are targets only. The predictor never receives them.

## Implementation staging

The first GPU run used $W=64$, rank 64, and the top singular bases of the released aggregate J matrix. It was a cheaper J-subspace diagnostic, not the literal per-horizon $J_\Delta$ residual specified below. [`docs/audits/job_45.md`](../../docs/audits/job_45.md) found validation conditional-mean signal but no nonlinear or causal success. The next diagnostic keeps this reduced setting while repairing checkpoint selection, document provenance, prefix-invariance checks, and fixed-future effect metrics. Fitting the full $J_\Delta$ path waits until those seams pass.

## Relation to the Jacobian lens

The Jacobian-lens result is the motivating observation: an earlier middle-layer state has a stable average linear relationship to computations expressed at later final-layer positions. LUCID3 asks whether a learned nonlinear predictor can replace that population-averaged closed form with a prompt-conditioned prediction.

This is deliberately not a nonlinear Jacobian estimator. It predicts future states, not intervention derivatives.

For each horizon $\Delta$, a mean Jacobian provides a fixed first-order starting path:

$$
J_\Delta
=\mathbb E_{x,t}
\left[\frac{\partial h_{L,t+\Delta}}{\partial h_{M,t}}\right].
$$

A centered affine use of $J_\Delta$ is a sensitivity-derived baseline and residual connection:

$$
\hat h^{J}_{L,t+\Delta}
=\mu_L+J_\Delta(h_{M,t}-\mu_M).
$$

Because a sensitivity is not an absolute-state regression coefficient, a learned affine map with the same source and target is a required stronger linear baseline. An identical GRU trained from the horizon mean rather than the J path tests whether the fixed J path helps at all.

## Exact prediction row

Use frozen `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` at revision `851bf6e806efd8d0a36b00ddf55e13ccb7b8cd0a`.

For one WikiText document window of $W+K$ tokens:

- teacher computation may inspect all $W+K$ tokens to construct labels;
- predictor input is $X=H_{M,1:W}\in\mathbb R^{W\times d}$;
- predictor target is $Y=H_{L,W+1:W+K}\in\mathbb R^{K\times d}$;
- tokens and hidden states at positions $W+1:W+K$ have no path into the predictor forward pass.

$H_M$ is post-middle-block residual. $H_L$ is post-final-block and pre-final-RMSNorm.

Starting values are $W=128$, $K=8$, and latent rank 256. They are small engineering choices inherited from the prior context, not tuned scientific thresholds. Every row is a full window with position IDs reset consistently, so the horizon mean is also the relative-position-conditioned mean.

## Deterministic phase

The smallest useful experiment estimates the conditional mean:

$$
f_\theta(X)_\Delta
\approx\mathbb E[h_{L,t+\Delta}\mid H_{M,\le t}=X].
$$

Architecture:

1. project each observed middle state to rank 256;
2. causally encode the $W$ observed states with one GRU;
3. combine the final GRU state with a learned horizon embedding;
4. write a nonlinear residual on top of the fixed $J_\Delta$ path.

Train with one loss: MSE standardized by horizon-specific feature scales $\sigma_{L,\Delta}\in\mathbb R^d$, then averaged equally over batch, horizon, and feature. The source mean is estimated from the last observed middle state only; target means and scales are estimated separately for each horizon. Qwen and $J_\Delta$ remain frozen.

This phase does not model the full conditional distribution. MSE can average incompatible continuations and produce off-manifold hidden states. That is an explicit limitation, not a reason to add diffusion before testing whether conditional nonlinear signal exists.

## Baselines

Legal predictors receive the same information and target:

1. train mean by horizon;
2. centered fixed $J_\Delta$ by horizon;
3. learned affine map from current $h_{M,t}$ to each horizon;
4. nonlinear last-state model using the same horizon decoder as the recurrent model but no prefix encoder;
5. validation-sized linear recurrence $z_\tau=Az_{\tau-1}+Bx_\tau$ with one linear readout $C_\Delta z_W+b_\Delta$ per horizon;
6. nonlinear GRU residual on the horizon mean;
7. nonlinear GRU residual on the fixed J path.

These comparisons ask separately whether history helps, whether nonlinearity helps, and whether the J path helps. The headline future-prediction result is against affine-last, nonlinear-last, and linear-prefix. The specific “nonlinear addition to J” claim additionally requires the J-based GRU to improve on the otherwise identical mean-based GRU.

## Evaluation

Report by future horizon, document, and seed:

- raw hidden-state MSE;
- train-standardized MSE;
- mean-centered hidden-state cosine using the training mean for that horizon;
- $D_{KL}(p_{\mathrm{teacher}}\|p_{\mathrm{prediction}})$ after frozen final RMSNorm and unembedding.

The output KL is a diagnostic for whether a mean hidden state retains the teacher continuation's predictive distribution. It is not a calibrated likelihood for the unknown future.

Use paired document bootstrap intervals for method differences. Report three independent training seeds and the seed-specific effects rather than treating windows as independent. Validation fixes $W$, $K$, sample count, stopping, and checkpoint selection before the test split is opened once. Wide intervals from the small official test document count are reported rather than hidden by window-level resampling.

## Leakage checks

- Split by official WikiText document IDs before constructing windows and assert train, validation, and test are pairwise disjoint.
- Never construct train and test windows from the same document; audit long exact overlaps across documents.
- Log the first decoded train and validation rows with the exact input/target boundary.
- Pass the teacher's causal attention mask and position IDs explicitly when constructing labels.
- Trace the model forward graph and assert no future token, future $H_M$, or any $H_L$ is an input.
- Fit Jacobians, centering, and scaling on training documents only.
- Reset recurrent state at every window; use full windows or mask padding.
- Train a shuffled-target negative control by permuting $Y$ across documents within each horizon. It must not outperform the horizon mean on validation.
- Evaluate every metric by horizon so a one-token alignment error is visible.

## What would count as useful

The predeclared primary score is equally weighted standardized MSE over horizons $\Delta=2\ldots K$; $\Delta=1$ is reported but cannot alone establish multi-step prediction.

A useful deterministic result requires the J-based GRU to improve on:

- the per-horizon affine-last predictor;
- the decoder-matched nonlinear last-state predictor;
- the linear-prefix model;

on the primary score over held-out documents. This would show that both the observed trajectory and nonlinear conditioning carry predictive information about later final states. Improvement over the identical mean-based GRU is a separate requirement for claiming that the J path helps.

It would not show that the model represents multimodal futures, rolls out coherently, supports interventions, or plans.

## Stochastic follow-up

Conditional diffusion is earned only if the deterministic model contains predictive signal but its mean predictions appear off manifold—for example, hidden MSE improves while cosine or frozen-head diagnostics remain poor.

The follow-up would model:

$$
p_\theta(H_{L,t+1:t+K}\mid H_{M,\le t})
$$

in a reduced residual/J subspace and compare proper sample-based scores. Diffusion is not part of the first implementation.

## Main risks

- Future final states depend strongly on unknown future tokens, so the conditional mean may be intrinsically blurry.
- WikiText may provide insufficient repeated contexts to identify useful multimodal structure.
- The current middle state may already summarize nearly all useful prefix information; then the GRU should not beat the pointwise MLP.
- A learned affine map may explain nearly all predictable signal, falsifying the need for nonlinearity.
- Hidden-state MSE can reward shared topic, position, or residual directions rather than continuation-specific content. Horizon-specific standardization, centered cosine, the horizon mean, and the shuffled-target control expose different parts of this failure.
- The model may partially reconstruct typical future token identity without learning a compact trajectory state. That is still future prediction, but not yet the intended world-state abstraction. A diagnostic oracle given the forbidden true future token embedding measures how much target variance token identity can explain; it is not a legal baseline.

## Plan

- [ ] goal: construct leak-free WikiText future-state rows
  - [ ] cache frozen middle-prefix inputs and final-future targets with document provenance
  - [ ] log decoded boundary examples and exact tensor shapes
  - failure modes: future middle states enter input; off-by-one token target; overlapping document split
  - deliverable: smoke log proving the predictor sees only positions $\le t$
- [ ] goal: establish linear and pointwise predictive baselines
  - [ ] fit $J_\Delta$, affine-last, decoder-matched nonlinear-last, and linear-prefix controls
  - [ ] report horizon-resolved validation metrics
  - failure modes: Jacobian treated as state regression; baseline receives less context unintentionally
  - deliverable: one baseline table from the common training entry point
- [ ] goal: test nonlinear conditional mean prediction
  - [ ] train J-based and mean-based GRU-prefix residual predictors with the same architecture and one loss
  - [ ] freeze protocol and evaluate untouched test documents for three seeds
  - failure modes: gain exists only at $\Delta=1$; recurrence ignored; mean state leaves useful manifold
  - deliverable: held-out horizon table with paired document-bootstrap intervals

## UAT

| Scenario | Interpretation | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| useful first result | J-based GRU beats affine-last, decoder-matched nonlinear-last, and linear-prefix on the fixed $\Delta=2\ldots K$ score | untouched-test horizon metrics and paired document-bootstrap intervals for three seeds |
| J-path result | J-based GRU also beats the identical mean-based GRU | same paired test comparison; otherwise the future predictor works but the J path did not help |
| linear result | affine-last or linear-prefix matches GRU | conditional prediction is valid, but nonlinearity is not earned |
| current-state result | nonlinear-last matches GRU | the middle-layer trajectory adds no evidence beyond $h_{M,t}$ |
| conditional-mean limitation | MSE improves but frozen-head diagnostics remain poor | consider stochastic prediction rather than adding more deterministic losses |
| null result | no learned predictor beats the horizon mean materially | stop before diffusion or planning work; first audit leakage, alignment, and optimization |

To introduce the J lens paper here is the form conceptually relevent potion of the paper in my (wassname) opinion

    ```tex
    \section{Methods}\label{methods}

    A transformer-based language model processes its input as a sequence of token positions. At each position, the model maintains a vector called the residual stream, which serves as a shared memory that every layer reads from and writes to \cite{nelhage2021mathematical}. The value of the residual stream vector is progressively updated across the model's layers. The residual stream at the first layer encodes little more than the identity of the current token; by the final layer, it has been transformed into a representation from which the model's next-token prediction can be read off directly, by multiplying it with a fixed unembedding matrix $W_U$ that maps residual-stream vectors to scores over the vocabulary. The layers in between perform the model's computation, incrementally enriching the residual stream with internally computed information. The Jacobian lens is a technique for inspecting the contents of the residual stream at these intermediate layers.

    \begin{figure}[!t]
        \centering
        \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth,height=0.7\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_009_gdoc.png}
        \caption{\label{jlens-schematic} The Jacobian lens. (A) $J_\ell$ is computed by backpropagating from the final-layer residual stream to $h_\ell$ and averaging the resulting Jacobians over token positions and over a corpus of prompts. (B) Reading from the lens replaces all layers downstream of $\ell$ with the single linear map $J_\ell$ followed by the model's own unembedding, yielding a ranked list of vocabulary tokens for the activation at that layer. (C) Patching in lens coordinates reads the activation's projections onto two J-lens vectors, applies a permutation $\sigma$ to those coordinates, and writes the result back, leaving unchanged the component of the activation that is orthogonal to those two vectors.}
    \end{figure}

    \subsection{The Jacobian Lens}\label{methods-jlens}

    The basic idea is to characterize an intermediate activation vector by its first-order causal effect on the model's outputs, over a broad distribution of potential contexts. Consider the residual stream $h_\ell$ at layer $\ell$ and some token position $t$. A small perturbation to $h_\ell$ will propagate through the remaining layers and shift the final-layer residual stream $h_{\text{final},t'}$ at every position $t' \geq t$. To first order, this relationship is linear, and is described by the Jacobian matrix $\partial h_{\text{final},t'} / \partial h_{\ell,t}$. Composing this Jacobian with the unembedding layer yields the first-order effect of the perturbation on the model's output logits at position $t'$.

    A Jacobian computed on a single prompt, however, conflates two kinds of structure: the model's general disposition to verbalize a given concept, and the particular use to which that concept is being put in the current context. We isolate the former component by averaging within and across contexts. For each layer $\ell$, we compute

    $$ J_\ell \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{\,t,\,t' \geq t,\,\text{prompt}} \left[ \frac{\partial h_{\text{final},t'}}{\partial h_{\ell,t}} \right], $$

    where the expectation is taken over the source position $t$, all subsequent positions $t'$ within the context, and a corpus of one thousand prompts sampled from a pretraining-like distribution. The result is a single $d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix per layer that maps from a source layer $\ell$ to the final layer $L$.

    Applying the lens to an activation $h_\ell$ is equivalent to replacing all subsequent layers with the appropriate lens matrix, followed by the normal unembedding operations (typically normalization, then multiplication by the unembedding matrix $W_U$):

    $$ \text{lens}(h_\ell) \;= \text{softmax}(W_U \, \text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell)) $$

    This produces a score for every token in the model's vocabulary. Sorting these scores and inspecting the top entries gives a human-readable description of the activation: a short list of words that the activation is, on average across contexts, disposed to make the model say. We refer to the rows of $W_U J_\ell$ as the \textit{Jacobian} \textit{lens }(J-lens) vectors at layer $\ell$; each J-lens vector is a direction in residual-stream space associated with a single token in the model's vocabulary.

    The averaged Jacobian, applied to a given activation vector, measures the effect on present and future outputs that the vector might have across the range of contexts the model encounters. The highly weighted output tokens, those that ``appear in the lens,'' are therefore represented in a \textit{verbalizable }format. We examine several variants of the Jacobian lens methodology (e.g. computing only present and not future token effects, freezing attention patterns while computing Jacobians, and varying the number of contexts over which we average) in \S\ref{app-method-details}; our qualitative results are robust to these choices.
    ```

1. `docs/pseudocode/conditional_future_residual_predictor.py` defines the method.
2. `slop/specs/20260829_conditional_future_residual_predictor.md` defines the experiment and failure tests.

If prose and pseudocode disagree, stop and resolve the disagreement before implementation.

## Research rules

- Freeze the language model.
- Split WikiText by official document ID before constructing windows.
- Fit Jacobians, centering, scaling, and learned models on training documents only.
- Prove that no future token, future middle state, or final state enters the predictor forward graph.
- Report every metric by future horizon.
- Keep one driving training loss.
- The current runner is an aggregate-J-basis diagnostic, not the final per-horizon $J_\Delta$ experiment; label its results accordingly.
- Compare with horizon mean, fixed-basis last-state, linear-prefix, random-basis, and shuffled-target controls before adding the full $J_\Delta$ path.
- Run a cross-document shuffled-target control; it must collapse to the horizon mean.
- Treat fixed-future token edits as exploratory sensitivity tests; causal success requires effect error below the zero-effect baseline with uncertainty.
- Treat deterministic MSE as conditional-mean estimation, not conditional-density estimation.
- Do not add diffusion until a deterministic predictor shows signal and an observed mean-prediction limitation.
- Do not add interventions, actions, planning, or open-loop rollout to the first experiment.
- Fail on missing fields, bad tensor shapes, non-finite values, or non-causal inputs.
- Use `uv`, `just`, loguru, jaxtyping, and beartype when implementation starts.
- Run GPU work through pueue.
- Put draft reviews, audits, and abandoned designs in `slop/`.

Separate observations from inferences. Quote sources rather than laundering claims through summaries. Sign agent-authored prose and comments with the agent name.

# LUCID3 conditional future-residual predictor — pseudocode, not runnable code.
# Method draft by Codex from wassname's proposal and scientist-panel corrections.

qwen, tokenize = load("Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B", revision="851bf6e806efd8d0a36b00ddf55e13ccb7b8cd0a")
qwen.freeze()
L, d = qwen.n_layers, qwen.hidden_size
M, r = L // 2, 256
W, K = 128, 8                                     # observed prefix, future horizon
train_docs, val_docs, test_docs = wikitext_103_document_splits()
train_windows = full_document_windows(train_docs, length=W + K)
val_windows = full_document_windows(val_docs, length=W + K)
test_windows = full_document_windows(test_docs, length=W + K)


def teacher_states(tokens, attention_mask, position_ids):
    H_M, H_L = qwen.residual_outputs(
        tokens, layers=[M, L - 1], attention_mask=attention_mask, position_ids=position_ids
    )
    return H_M.detach(), H_L.detach()              # each ∈ ℝ^{b×(W+K)×d}


def forecast_row(document_window):
    tokens, attention_mask, position_ids = tokenize_full_window(document_window, W + K)
    H_M, H_L = teacher_states(tokens, attention_mask, position_ids)
    X = H_M[:, :W]                                 # predictor input stops here
    Y = H_L[:, W:W + K]                            # actual future targets
    input_mask = attention_mask[:, :W]
    assert_no_predictor_input(tokens[:, W:], H_M[:, W:], H_L)
    return ForecastRow(X=X, Y=Y, attention_mask=input_mask, document_id=document_window.id)


train_rows = map(forecast_row, train_windows)
val_rows = map(forecast_row, val_windows)
test_rows = map(forecast_row, test_windows)
μ_M_last = mean(last_state(train_rows.X), dim="rows")                 # ∈ ℝ^d
μ_L_Δ, σ_L_Δ = target_statistics_by_horizon(train_rows.Y)             # ∈ ℝ^{K×d}
assert all(σ_L_Δ > 0)


# J_Δ is a sensitivity baseline, not a state-regression coefficient.
J_Δ = fit_mean_jacobian_by_offset(qwen, train_windows, source_layer=M, horizons=1..K)


def horizon_mean(X):
    return broadcast_rows(μ_L_Δ, X.batch)                             # ∈ ℝ^{b×K×d}


def j_base(X):
    h_now = last_state(X)
    return stack([
        μ_L_Δ[Δ - 1] + (h_now - μ_M_last) @ J_Δ[Δ].T
        for Δ in 1..K
    ], dim="horizon")


# Each base-path variant owns an independently trained correction model.
def make_gru_predictor(base_path):
    reader = Linear(d, r)
    encoder = GRU(input_size=r, hidden_size=r)
    horizon_embedding = Embedding(K, r)
    conditioner = MLP(2 * r, r)
    writer = Linear(r, d, init=zeros)

    def predict(X, attention_mask):
        Z = encoder.causal_scan(reader(X), attention_mask)
        z_now = last_nonpadding(Z)
        correction = stack([
            writer(conditioner(concat(z_now, horizon_embedding[Δ - 1])))
            for Δ in 1..K
        ], dim="horizon")
        return base_path(X) + correction

    return predict


gru_J = make_gru_predictor(j_base)                  # proposed nonlinear addition to J
mean_gru = make_gru_predictor(horizon_mean)          # same model without J path


def state_loss(Y_hat, Y):
    return mean(((Y_hat - Y) / σ_L_Δ) ** 2)          # equal batch/horizon/feature weight


# The last-state nonlinear control reuses the same decoder but has no prefix encoder.
baselines = fit_on_train_select_on_validation({
    "horizon_mean": fixed_predictor(horizon_mean),
    "J_by_horizon": fixed_predictor(j_base),
    "affine_last": affine_per_horizon(last_state_only=True),
    "nonlinear_last": same_decoder_without_prefix_encoder(r),
    "linear_prefix": validation_sized_linear_rnn(),
    "mean_gru": mean_gru,
    "gru_J": gru_J,
}, loss=state_loss)


for model in learned(baselines):
    for X, Y, attention_mask in batches(train_rows):
        Y_hat = model(X, attention_mask)
        loss = state_loss(Y_hat, Y)
        model.parameters ← optimizer_step(model.parameters, ∇(loss, model.parameters))
        log(model.name, loss, raw_mse(Y_hat, Y), centered_cosine(Y_hat, Y, μ_L_Δ))


def final_logits(H):
    return qwen.unembed(qwen.final_rmsnorm(H))


def evaluate(rows):
    for X, Y, attention_mask in rows:
        for name, Y_hat in apply(baselines, X, attention_mask):
            for Δ in 1..K:
                report(name, Δ, raw_mse(Y_hat[:, Δ - 1], Y[:, Δ - 1]))
                report(name, Δ, standardized_mse(Y_hat[:, Δ - 1], Y[:, Δ - 1]))
                report(name, Δ, centered_cosine(
                    Y_hat[:, Δ - 1], Y[:, Δ - 1], μ_L_Δ[Δ - 1]
                ))
                report(name, Δ, kl_teacher_pred(
                    final_logits(Y[:, Δ - 1]), final_logits(Y_hat[:, Δ - 1])
                ))


# Target-shuffle control preserves each horizon marginal but destroys X–Y dependence.
shuffled_train = permute_Y_across_documents_within_horizon(train_rows)
shuffle_gru = train(make_gru_predictor(horizon_mean), shuffled_train, loss=state_loss)
assert_not_better_than(shuffle_gru, horizon_mean, split=val_rows)


# Diagnostic oracles receive forbidden future information and are never legal baselines.
report_true_future_token_embedding_oracle(val_rows)
report_qwen_source_next_token_entropy_strata(val_rows, horizon=1)


assert pairwise_disjoint_document_ids(train_docs, val_docs, test_docs)
audit_long_exact_train_test_overlaps()
compare("gru_J", "nonlinear_last")                 # value of observed trajectory
compare("gru_J", "linear_prefix")                  # value of nonlinearity
compare("gru_J", "affine_last")                    # value beyond simple prediction
compare("gru_J", "mean_gru")                       # value of fixed J path


# Validation freezes model sizes, sample count, stopping, and the primary score.
# Primary score: equally weighted standardized MSE over horizons 2..K.
protocol = freeze_protocol_from_validation(primary_horizons=2..K)
for seed in three_independent_training_seeds:
    train_and_select_on_train_val(seed)
    evaluate(protocol.untouched_test_rows_once())
report_per_horizon_seed_and_paired_document_bootstrap()

# Decision rule:
# - Better mean prediction is not a learned conditional density.
# - GRU > nonlinear-last and linear-prefix supports trajectory + nonlinear information.
# - gru_J > mean_gru supports the specific claim that the J path helps.
# - A deterministic win with poor manifold diagnostics earns a stochastic follow-up.
# - No intervention, world-model, or planning claim is made in this experiment.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:194:We perform an extensive empirical study across 8 domains that include continuous and discrete actions, visual and low-dimensional inputs, dense and sparse rewards, different reward scales, 2D and 3D worlds, and procedural generation. [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") summarizes the benchmark results, showing that Dreamer outperforms a wide range of previous expert algorithms across diverse domains. Crucially, Dreamer substantially outperforms PPO across all domains.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-195-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-196-*   •Atari This established benchmark contains 57 Atari 2600 games with a budget of 200M frames, posing a diverse range of challenges[38](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib38). We use the sticky action simulator setting [39](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib39). Dreamer outperforms the powerful MuZero algorithm[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8) while using only a fraction of the computational resources. Dreamer also outperforms the widely-used expert algorithms Rainbow [40](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib40) and IQN [41](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib41).

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-206-Collecting diamonds in the popular game Minecraft has been a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence[18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). Every episode in this game is set in a unique randomly generated and infinite 3D world. Episodes last until the player dies or up to 36000 steps equaling 30 minutes, during which the player needs to discover a sequence of 12 items from sparse rewards by foraging for resources and crafting tools. It takes about 20 minutes for experienced human players to obtain diamonds[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). We follow the block breaking setting of prior work [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19) because the provided action space would make it challenging for stochastic policies to keep a key pressed for a prolonged time.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-207-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:208:Because of the training time in this complex domain, extensive tuning would be difficult for Minecraft. Instead, we apply Dreamer out of the box with its default hyperparameters. As shown in [Figures 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") and[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without using human data as was required by VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) or adaptive curricula[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19). All the Dreamer agents we trained on Minecraft discover diamonds in 100M environment steps. While several strong baselines progress to advanced items such as the iron pickaxe, none of them discovers a diamond.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-210-#### Ablations
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-211-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:212:In [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), we ablate the robustness techniques and learning signals on a diverse set of 14 tasks to understand their importance. The training curves of individual tasks are included in the supplementary material. We observe that all robustness techniques contribute to performance, most notably the KL objective of the world model, followed by return normalization and symexp twohot regression for reward and value prediction. In general, we find that each individual technique is critical on a subset of tasks but may not affect performance on other tasks.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-213-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:214:To investigate the effect of the world model, we ablate the learning signals of Dreamer by stopping either the task-specific reward and value prediction gradients or the task-agnostic reconstruction gradients from shaping its representations. Unlike previous reinforcement learning algorithms that often rely only on task-specific learning signals[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), Dreamer rests predominantly on the unsupervised objective of its world model. This finding could allow for future algorithm variants that leverage pretraining on unsupervised data.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-215-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-216-#### Scaling properties
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-217-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:218:To investigate whether Dreamer can scale robustly, we train 6 model sizes ranging from 12M to 400M parameters, as well as different replay ratios on Crafter [50](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib50) and a DMLab task[43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). The replay ratio affects the number of gradient updates performed by the agent. [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") shows robust learning with fixed hyperparameters across the compared model sizes and replay ratios. Moreover, increasing the model size directly translates to both higher task performance and a lower data requirement. Increasing the number of gradient steps further reduces the interactions needed to learn successful behaviors. The results show that Dreamer learns robustly across model sizes and replay ratios and that its performance and provides a predictable way for increasing performance given computational resources.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-220-## Previous work
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-221-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:222:Developing general-purpose algorithms has long been a goal of reinforcement learning research. PPO [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5) is one of the most widely used algorithms and is relatively robust but requires large amounts of experience and often yields lower performance than specialized alternatives. SAC [32](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib32) is a popular choice for continuous control and leverages experience replay for data-efficiency, but in practice requires tuning, especially for its entropy scale, and struggles under high-dimensional inputs [51](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib51). MuZero [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8) plans using a value prediction model and has been applied to board games and Atari, but the authors did not release an implementation and the algorithm contains several complex components, making it challenging to reproduce. Gato [52](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib52) fits one large model to expert demonstrations of multiple tasks, but is only applicable when expert data is available. In comparison, Dreamer masters a diverse range of environments with fixed hyperparameters, does not require expert data, and its implementation is open source.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-223-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-224-Minecraft has been a focus of recent research. With MALMO [53](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib53), Microsoft released a free version of the successful game for research purposes. MineRL [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18) offers several competition environments, which we rely on as the basis for our experiments. The MineRL competition supports agents in exploring and learning meaningful skills through a diverse human dataset [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18). Voyager obtains items at a similar depth in the technology tree as Dreamer using API calls to a language model but operates on top of the MineFlayer bot scripting layer that was specifically engineered to the game and exposes high-level actions[54](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib54). VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) trained an agent to play Minecraft through behavioral cloning based on expert data of keyboard and mouse actions collected by contractors and finetuning using reinforcement learning to obtain diamonds using 720 GPUs for 9 days. In comparison, Dreamer uses the MineRL competition action space to autonomously learn to collect diamonds from sparse rewards using 1 GPU for 9 days, without human data.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-226-## Conclusion
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-227-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:228:We present the third generation of the Dreamer algorithm, a general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters a wide range of domains with fixed hyperparameters. Dreamer excels not only across over 150 tasks but also learns robustly across varying data and compute budgets, moving reinforcement learning toward a wide range of practical applications. Applied out of the box, Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch, achieving a significant milestone in the field of artificial intelligence. As a high-performing algorithm that is based on a learned world model, Dreamer paves the way for future research directions, including teaching agents world knowledge from internet videos and learning a single world model across domains to allow artificial agents to build up increasingly general knowledge and competency.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:307:We employ the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5), which has become a standard choice in the field, to compare Dreamer under fixed hyperparameters across all benchmarks. There are a large number of PPO implementations available publicly and they are known to substantially vary in task performance [55](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib55). To ensure a comparison that is representative of the highest performance PPO can achieve under fixed hyperparameters across domains, we choose the high-quality PPO implementation available in the Acme framework [56](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib56) and select its hyperparameters in [Baselines](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Ax1.SSx1 "Baselines ‣ Methods ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") following recommendations [55](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib55), [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib13) and additionally tune its epoch batch size to be large enough for complex environments [42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42), its learning rate, and its entropy scale. We match the discount factor to Dreamer because it works well across domains and is a common choice in the literature [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib35), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8). We choose the IMPALA network architecture that we have found performed better than alternatives [42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42) and set the minibatch size to the largest possible for one A100 GPU. We verify the performance of our PPO implementation and hyperparameters on the ProcGen benchmark, where a highly tuned PPO implementation has been reported by the PPO authors [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). We find that our implementation matches or slightly outperforms this performance reference.

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:14:World models learn general knowledge from videos and simulate experience for training be-haviors in imagination, offering a path towards intelligent agents. However, previous world models have been unable to accurately predict object interactions in complex environments. We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve control tasks by reinforcement learning inside of a fast and accurate world model. In the complex video game Minecraft, the world model accurately predicts object interactions and game mechanics, outperforming previous world models by a large margin. The world model achieves real-time interactive inference on a single GPU through a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture. Moreover, the world model learns general action conditioning from only a small amount of data, allowing it to extract the majority of its knowledge from diverse unlabeled videos. We propose the challenge of obtaining diamonds in Minecraft from only offline data, aligning with practical applications such as robotics where learning from environment inter-action can be unsafe and slow. This task requires choosing sequences of over 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from raw pixels. By learning behaviors in imagination, Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without environment interaction. Our work provides a scalable recipe for imagination training, marking a step towards intelligent agents. Agent task: Gather wood

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:40:To solve complex tasks in embodied environments, intelligent agents need to deeply understand the world and choose successful actions. World models offer a promising approach towards this goal by learning to predict the future outcomes of potential actions from the perspective of an agent, such as a robot or a video game player. This way, world models equip agents with a deep understanding of the world and the ability to choose actions by planning or reinforcement learning in imagination. Moreover, world models can in principle learn from fixed datasets, allowing to train agents purely in imagination without the need for online interaction. Optimizing behaviors offline is valuable for many practical applications, such as robots in the physical world, where online interaction with a partially trained agent is often unsafe. World model agents, such as Dreamer 3, are among the best-performing and most robust rein-forcement learning algorithms for games and robotics to date 1–6 . While these models are fast and accurate for their narrow environments, their architecture lacks the ability to fit complex real world distributions. Controllable video models, such as Genie 3, have been trained on diverse real video and games and have accomplished diverse scene generation and simple interactions 7–12 . These models are based on scalable architectures, such as diffusion transformers 13,14 . However, they still struggle to learn the precise physics of object interactions and game mechanics, limiting their use-fulness for training successful agents. Moreover, they often require many GPUs to simulate a single scene in real time, further reducing their practicality for imagination training. We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that solves control tasks by imagination training inside of a fast and accurate world model. Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in the challeng-ing video game Minecraft purely from a standard offline dataset, without environment interaction. Dreamer 4 leverages a novel shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture to ac-curately learn complex object interactions while enabling real-time human interaction and efficient imagination training. We show that the world model accurately predicts a wide range of seman-tic interactions in Minecraft, outperforming previous world models by a large margin. Moreover, Dreamer 4 can be trained on large amounts of unlabeled videos and requires only a small amount of videos paired with actions. This opens up the possibility of learning general world knowledge from diverse web videos in the future, for which action labels are not available. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve challenging control tasks by imag-ination training inside of a world model. • Dreamer 4 is the first agent to collect diamonds in Minecraft from only offline data, substantially improving over OpenAI’s VPT offline agent 15 despite using 100 × less data. • We introduce a high-capacity world model that achieves real-time inference on a single GPU through a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture. • We show that the world model accurately predicts a wide range of object interactions and game mechanics in Minecraft, substantially outperforming previous world models. • We show that the world model can learn from unlabeled videos and requires only a small amount of aligned data to learn action conditioning with strong generalization. • An extensive ablation study measures the improvements of the objective and architecture.

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:281:We perform a wide range of experiments to evaluate and explore the capabilities of Dreamer 4. The majority of our experiments focus on Minecraft, a complex video game that features infinite open worlds including monsters and hundreds of items that can be mined or crafted, with raw pixel observations and low-level mouse and keyboard actions. We primarily use the VPT dataset 15 that contains 2541 hours of contractor gameplay with 360p video and mouse and keyboard actions at 20 FPS. The experiments are designed to answer the following questions: • Does Dreamer 4 learn to solve challenging control tasks purely by imagination training inside the world model, without online environment interaction? (Section 4.1) • How well does Dreamer 4 learn to predict accurate object interactions and game mechanics in Minecraft compared to previous world models? (Section 4.2) • How much action data does Dreamer 4 need for learning action conditioning, and how far does the learned action grounding generalize? (Section 4.3) • To what extent does each component of its objective and architecture contribute to the perfor-mance of Dreamer 4? (Section 4.4) We train models with 2B parameters—400M for the tokenizer and 1.6B for the dynamics model—on 256 to 1024 TPU-v5p with batch size 1 per device and FSDP sharding 44,45 . To improve generations without context, we treat 30% of the videos in the batch as separate images, effectively training the dynamics model to generate start frames. For Minecraft, we use 256 spatial tokens with 192 frames context length and 256 batch length. For the real world datasets, we use 512 spatial tokens with 96 frames context length and 128 batch length.

Every episode in this game is set in a unique randomly generated and infinite 3D world. Episodes last until the player dies or up to 36000 steps equaling 30 minutes, during which the player needs to discover a sequence of 12 items from sparse rewards by foraging for resources and crafting tools. It takes about 20 minutes for experienced human players to obtain diamonds[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). We follow the block breaking setting of prior work [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19) because the provided action space would make it challenging for stochastic policies to keep a key pressed for a prolonged time.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-207-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:208:Because of the training time in this complex domain, extensive tuning would be difficult for Minecraft. Instead, we apply Dreamer out of the box with its default hyperparameters. As shown in [Figures 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") and[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without using human data as was required by VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) or adaptive curricula[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19). All the Dreamer agents we trained on Minecraft discover diamonds in 100M environment steps. While several strong baselines progress to advanced items such as the iron pickaxe, none of them discovers a diamond.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:212:In [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), we ablate the robustness techniques and learning signals on a diverse set of 14 tasks to understand their importance. The training curves of individual tasks are included in the supplementary material. We observe that all robustness techniques contribute to performance, most notably the KL objective of the world model, followed by return normalization and symexp twohot regression for reward and value prediction. In general, we find that each individual technique is critical on a subset of tasks but may not affect performance on other tasks.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:214:To investigate the effect of the world model, we ablate the learning signals of Dreamer by stopping either the task-specific reward and value prediction gradients or the task-agnostic reconstruction gradients from shaping its representations. Unlike previous reinforcement learning algorithms that often rely only on task-specific learning signals[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), Dreamer rests predominantly on the unsupervised objective of its world model. docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-216-#### Scaling properties
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-217-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:218:To investigate whether Dreamer can scale robustly, we train 6 model sizes ranging from 12M to 400M parameters, as well as different replay ratios on Crafter [50](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib50) and a DMLab task[43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). The replay ratio affects the number of gradient updates performed by the agent. [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") shows robust learning with fixed hyperparameters across the compared model sizes and replay ratios. Moreover, increasing the model size directly translates to both higher task performance and a lower data requirement. Increasing the number of gradient steps further reduces the interactions needed to learn successful behaviors. The results show that Dreamer learns robustly across model sizes and replay ratios and that its performance and provides a predictable way for increasing performance given computational resources.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-220-## Previous work
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-221-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:222:Developing general-purpose algorithms has long been a goal of reinforcement learning research. PPO [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5) is one of the most widely used algorithms and is relatively robust but requires large amounts of experience and often yields lower performance than specialized alternatives. SAC [32](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib32) is a popular choice for continuous control and leverages experience replay for data-efficiency, but in practice requires tuning, especially for its entropy scale, and struggles under high-dimensional inputs [51](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib51). MuZero [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8) plans using a value prediction model and has been applied to board games and Atari, but the authors did not release an implementation and the algorithm contains several complex components, making it challenging to reproduce. Gato [52](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib52) fits one large model to expert demonstrations of multiple tasks, but is only applicable when expert data is available. In comparison, Dreamer masters a diverse range of environments with fixed hyperparameters, does not require expert data, and its implementation is open source.
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-223-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-224-Minecraft has been a focus of recent research. With MALMO [53](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib53), Microsoft released a free version of the successful game for research purposes. MineRL [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18) offers several competition environments, which we rely on as the basis for our experiments. The MineRL competition supports agents in exploring and learning meaningful skills through a diverse human dataset [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18). Voyager obtains items at a similar depth in the technology tree as Dreamer using API calls to a language model but operates on top of the MineFlayer bot scripting layer that was specifically engineered to the game and exposes high-level actions[54](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib54). VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) trained an agent to play Minecraft through behavioral cloning based on expert data of keyboard and mouse actions collected by contractors and finetuning using reinforcement learning to obtain diamonds using 720 GPUs for 9 days. In comparison, Dreamer uses the MineRL competition action space to autonomously learn to collect diamonds from sparse rewards using 1 GPU for 9 days, without human data.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-226-## Conclusion
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md-227-
docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:228:We present the third generation of the Dreamer algorithm, a general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters a wide range of domains with fixed hyperparameters. Dreamer excels not only across over 150 tasks but also learns robustly across varying data and compute budgets, moving reinforcement learning toward a wide range of practical applications. Applied out of the box, Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch, achieving a significant milestone in the field of artificial intelligence. As a high-performing algorithm that is based on a learned world model, Dreamer paves the way for future research directions, including teaching agents world knowledge from internet videos and learning a single world model across domains to allow artificial agents to build up increasingly general knowledge and competency.

docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:307:We employ the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5), which has become a standard choice in the field, to compare Dreamer under fixed hyperparameters across all benchmarks. There are a large number of PPO implementations available publicly and they are known to substantially vary in task performance [55](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib55). To ensure a comparison that is representative of the highest performance PPO can achieve under fixed hyperparameters across domains, we choose the high-quality PPO implementation available in the Acme framework [56](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib56) and select its hyperparameters in [Baselines](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Ax1.SSx1 "Baselines ‣ Methods ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") following recommendations [55](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib55), [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib13) and additionally tune its epoch batch size to be large enough for complex environments [42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42), its learning rate, and its entropy scale. We match the discount factor to Dreamer because it works well across domains and is a common choice in the literature [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib35), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8). We choose the IMPALA network architecture that we have found performed better than alternatives [42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42) and set the minibatch size to the largest possible for one A100 GPU. We verify the performance of our PPO implementation and hyperparameters on the ProcGen benchmark, where a highly tuned PPO implementation has been reported by the PPO authors [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). We find that our implementation matches or slightly outperforms this performance reference.

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:14:World models learn general knowledge from videos and simulate experience for training be-haviors in imagination, offering a path towards intelligent agents. However, previous world models have been unable to accurately predict object interactions in complex environments. We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve control tasks by reinforcement learning inside of a fast and accurate world model. In the complex video game Minecraft, the world model accurately predicts object interactions and game mechanics, outperforming previous world models by a large margin. The world model achieves real-time interactive inference on a single GPU through a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture. Moreover, the world model learns general action conditioning from only a small amount of data, allowing it to extract the majority of its knowledge from diverse unlabeled videos. We propose the challenge of obtaining diamonds in Minecraft from only offline data, aligning with practical applications such as robotics where learning from environment inter-action can be unsafe and slow. This task requires choosing sequences of over 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from raw pixels. By learning behaviors in imagination, Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without environment interaction. Our work provides a scalable recipe for imagination training, marking a step towards intelligent agents. Agent task: Gather wood

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md-39-
docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:40:To solve complex tasks in embodied environments, intelligent agents need to deeply understand the world and choose successful actions. World models offer a promising approach towards this goal by learning to predict the future outcomes of potential actions from the perspective of an agent, such as a robot or a video game player. This way, world models equip agents with a deep understanding of the world and the ability to choose actions by planning or reinforcement learning in imagination. Moreover, world models can in principle learn from fixed datasets, allowing to train agents purely in imagination without the need for online interaction. Optimizing behaviors offline is valuable for many practical applications, such as robots in the physical world, where online interaction with a partially trained agent is often unsafe. World model agents, such as Dreamer 3, are among the best-performing and most robust rein-forcement learning algorithms for games and robotics to date 1–6 . While these models are fast and accurate for their narrow environments, their architecture lacks the ability to fit complex real world distributions. Controllable video models, such as Genie 3, have been trained on diverse real video and games and have accomplished diverse scene generation and simple interactions 7–12 . These models are based on scalable architectures, such as diffusion transformers 13,14 . However, they still struggle to learn the precise physics of object interactions and game mechanics, limiting their use-fulness for training successful agents. Moreover, they often require many GPUs to simulate a single scene in real time, further reducing their practicality for imagination training. We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that solves control tasks by imagination training inside of a fast and accurate world model. Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in the challeng-ing video game Minecraft purely from a standard offline dataset, without environment interaction. Dreamer 4 leverages a novel shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture to ac-curately learn complex object interactions while enabling real-time human interaction and efficient imagination training. We show that the world model accurately predicts a wide range of seman-tic interactions in Minecraft, outperforming previous world models by a large margin. Moreover, Dreamer 4 can be trained on large amounts of unlabeled videos and requires only a small amount of videos paired with actions. This opens up the possibility of learning general world knowledge from diverse web videos in the future, for which action labels are not available. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We introduce Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve challenging control tasks by imag-ination training inside of a world model. • Dreamer 4 is the first agent to collect diamonds in Minecraft from only offline data, substantially improving over OpenAI’s VPT offline agent 15 despite using 100 × less data. • We introduce a high-capacity world model that achieves real-time inference on a single GPU through a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture. • We show that the world model accurately predicts a wide range of object interactions and game mechanics in Minecraft, substantially outperforming previous world models. • We show that the world model can learn from unlabeled videos and requires only a small amount of aligned data to learn action conditioning with strong generalization. • An extensive ablation study measures the improvements of the objective and architecture.

Dreamer 4 consists of a causal tokenizer and an interactive dynam-ics model, which both use the same block-causal transformer architecture. The tokenizer encodes partially masked image patches and latent tokens, squeezes the latents through a low-dimensional projection with tanh activation, and decodes the patches. We present Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve complex control tasks by reinforcement learn-ing inside of a fast and accurate world model. The agent consists of a tokenizer and a dynamics model, as shown in Figure 2. The tokenizer compresses video frames into continuous representations and the dy-namics model predicts the representations given in-terleaved actions, both using the same efficient trans-former architecture. The tokenizer is trained using masked autoencoding and the dynamics is trained us-ing a shortcut forcing objective to enable interactive generations with a small number of forward passes and prevent accumulating errors over time. As out-lined in Algorithm 1, we first pretrain the tokenizer and world model on videos and actions, then finetune the policy and reward model into the world model by interleaving task embeddings, and finally post-train the policy through imagination training. To train a single dynamics transformer with multiple modalities and output heads, we normalize all loss terms by run-ning estimates of their root-mean-square (RMS).

docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:281:We perform a wide range of experiments to evaluate and explore the capabilities of Dreamer 4. The majority of our experiments focus on Minecraft, a complex video game that features infinite open worlds including monsters and hundreds of items that can be mined or crafted, with raw pixel observations and low-level mouse and keyboard actions. We primarily use the VPT dataset 15 that contains 2541 hours of contractor gameplay with 360p video and mouse and keyboard actions at 20 FPS. The experiments are designed to answer the following questions: • Does Dreamer 4 learn to solve challenging control tasks purely by imagination training inside the world model, without online environment interaction? (Section 4.1) • How well does Dreamer 4 learn to predict accurate object interactions and game mechanics in Minecraft compared to previous world models? (Section 4.2) • How much action data does Dreamer 4 need for learning action conditioning, and how far does the learned action grounding generalize? (Section 4.3) • To what extent does each component of its objective and architecture contribute to the perfor-mance of Dreamer 4? (Section 4.4) We train models with 2B parameters—400M for the tokenizer and 1.6B for the dynamics model—on 256 to 1024 TPU-v5p with batch size 1 per device and FSDP sharding 44,45 . To improve generations without context, we treat 30% of the videos in the batch as separate images, effectively training the dynamics model to generate start frames. For Minecraft, we use 256 spatial tokens with 192 frames context length and 256 batch length. For the real world datasets, we use 512 spatial tokens with 96 frames context length and 128 batch length.
