content.text:
# LUCID spec: a Dreamer world model read out of a frozen LLM

Status: the one system this repo builds. Written 2026-08-27 by CLAUDE from wassname's journal
(`docs/HUMAN_JOURNAL_summary.md`). Quoted lines are his. Code:
`src/lucid/train.py`. Data: `scripts/gen_roomworld.py` + `src/lucid/roomworld.py`.

## 1. Goal

> a pretrained model is a token level world model. but no latent space to plan on. the hope is to
> take dreamer which is next frame. then say we already have a strong world model with a
> different interface. and freeze it as it's too big, and learn a read, writer, and dynamics
> model. now if it works we have a nice latent space from the pretrained llm that we can plan on.
> all the rest, the dataset, setup, are all downstream of that goal.

> while dreamer does next frame we do next token
> where dreamer struggled to learn a world model, we struggle to extract an implicit world model
> while dreamer learns a small encoder, we learn a reader of a massive pretrained LLM
> while dreamer uses RL we use SFT / NLL / KL

> It should a) work for long trajectories b) be causal: e.g. if we swap something in the latent
> space the outcome / concept behind the outcome swaps, if we ablate a concept, we see outcomes
> drop out, and targeted because placebo or off target change does not have this effect

So: three small learned modules (read, step, write) around a frozen LLM, one training script, and
two demos as proof (section 7). Everything else is instrumentation.

## 2. The three ideas this rests on

### 2.1 A pretrained LLM is an implicit world model (wassname)

> The model has a next-token textual world model, but it is intractable. I want to extract it.
> Dreamer learns a world model for next-state prediction and then uses it for planning. I want
> to do something similar.

> The same frozen model playing both the user and assistant can work because we already have a
> world model. We need to learn a tractable latent state. That is hard in itself, but easier than
> learning a world model.

Why the write is residual, and why residual forces a next-state target. The residual stream
`hs` sits on a narrow manifold the frozen upper half accepts; writing an `hs` from scratch is out
of reach for a small module, so the write is a change, `hs_2 = hs_1 + hs_delta`. That opens a trap:
if the target is `hs_1` itself, `hs_delta = 0` is a perfect answer and every LUCID1 version that
used a same-position target found it. So the target is the next state, `hs_2`, a state the module
cannot reach without producing a real `hs_delta`. Here `hs_1` is the residual stream of the
question alone and `hs_2` is the residual stream of the question after the full history, so
`hs_delta` is what the history added and `z` is the only place it can come from.

> we are learning residual additions to hs_1 to predict hs_2, `hs_2 = hs_1 + write(read(hs_1))`,
> that's the only way I can see it working. Needs to be residual. And because it's residual,
> needs to be next-state decoding.

### 2.2 DreamerV3: latent dynamics you can imagine in (Hafner et al.)

> World models summarize an agent's experience into a predictive model that can be used in place
> of the environment to learn behaviors. When inputs are high-dimensional images, it is beneficial
> to learn compact state representations of the inputs to predict ahead in this learned latent
> space. These models are called latent dynamics models. Predicting ahead in latent space not only
> facilitates long-term predictions, it also allows to efficiently predict thousands of compact
> state sequences in parallel in a single batch, without having to generate images.
> -- DreamerV2 sec 2.1, `docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md`

DreamerV3 eq. 1 (RSSM): sequence model `h_t = f(h_{t-1}, z_{t-1}, a_{t-1})`, encoder (posterior)
`z_t ~ q(z | h_t, x_t)`, dynamics predictor (prior) `ẑ_t ~ p(z | h_t)`, decoder `x̂_t ~ p(x | h_t, z_t)`.
Two losses: reconstruction through the decoder, and the dynamics/representation KL between prior
and posterior. Imagination runs prior + sequence model only, with no decoder and no environment.

The mapping:

| Dreamer | LUCID | note |
|---|---|---|
| frame `x_t` | one history line `You go north. You are in the yard.` | a token-level world, one line per tick |
| action `a_t` | the action clause of the line, `You go north.` | mean of frozen token embeddings |
| encoder `q(z \| h, x)` | `read` of the frozen residual stream at the line's last token, then `post` GRU fold | reads hidden states, not text |
| dynamics predictor `p(z \| h)` | `step(z, a)` GRU | no observation; must predict the room from remembered map |
| decoder `p(x \| z)` | `write(z)` residual edit at the split layer, then the frozen upper half | the decoder is mostly frozen |
| reconstruction loss | KL(teacher with full context ‖ student with z only) at the answer tokens | section 5 |
| dynamics + representation KL | MSE between prior and stop-grad posterior, and the reverse at 0.1 | deterministic z, NextLat form |
| imagination | `step` k times, then one `post(0, prior)`, zero LLM forwards per imagined line | section 7.2 |

Where we deviate, and why each is forced by text rather than chosen:

- Next token (line), not next turn: "how do we backprop through 256 tokens without RL... just like
  Dreamer has video frames, we need next token."
- The decoder is residual off a real state, not a from-scratch reconstruction, with the
  next-state target of section 2.1.
- Deterministic z with MSE dynamics, not categorical z with KL: NextLat shows the next-latent
  prediction with a stop-grad target converges to a belief state; we take that verbatim.
  Stochastic z is a later addition, not a first requirement.
- Action conditioning by concatenation: "how can we plan over the latent state if it's not
  conditional on action? oh I guess we just append the action to the input."

### 2.3 J-space: which residual directions matter downstream (Gurnee, Sofroniew, Lindsey et al. 2026)

> For each layer ℓ, we compute J_ℓ = E_{t, t' ≥ t, prompt}[ ∂h_{final,t'} / ∂h_{ℓ,t} ], where the
> expectation is taken over the source position t, all subsequent positions t' within the
> context, and a corpus of one thousand prompts sampled from a pretraining-like distribution.
> -- `docs/papers/jacobian_lens_workspace.md`, Methods

> The J-space also has some of the structural signatures of a global workspace [...] it is
> mechanistically privileged: J-lens vectors compose with the model's weights, both upstream and
> downstream, more broadly than other representational vectors do.

wassname, 2026-08-26:

> Anthropic J lens did "learned a closed form J solution that measured the sensitivity of the
> middle layer residual stream at layer 50% toward the output in the last layer". So the
> sensitivity over layers and tokens downstream in the trajectory. This is like planning but it's
> limited and linear. [...] they essentially extracted a shitty latent space from just wikitext.
> could we do the same but non linear, using dreamer type planning.

What the J-lens is, before we use it. It is a sensitivity map: how much does the residual stream
at an early position and a middle layer (their default: layer 50%) move the residual stream at
later positions and the last layer. They compute it in closed form as an averaged Jacobian over
wikitext, so it is linear and does not depend on the prompt. Its top singular directions are
where a small change early has the largest effect late, and swapping a concept along one of
them changes the answer downstream (spider to ant, eight legs to six). That is a simpler form
of what this repo wants: a compact state at a middle layer whose changes propagate to later
tokens in a predictable way. The J-lens shows the map exists and is low rank; we want the
nonlinear, prompt-conditional version that a Dreamer-style model can plan in.

How J fits, in three places, none of them a new loss:

1. The write learns the conditional, nonlinear version of the same map. Training `write` by KL
   through the frozen upper half backpropagates `J^T` at every step (a VJP, the same thing
   wassname's vjp-steering does for one concept). J̄ is the linear, context-averaged version.
2. J̄ is the init basis. `J̄ = U S Vᵀ` at the split layer; the top-r columns of `V` are the layer-m
   directions with the largest average downstream effect. `read` starts as projection onto them
   and `write` starts writing into them, so both start in the causal subspace rather than at
   random. This replaces LUCID1's weight-SVD "S-space" init with the same "teleport partway"
   intent: "we could teleport partway toward the goal rather than learning both transforms from
   random initialization." Logged check at init: fraction of `‖d_true‖²` inside span(V_r) against a
   random r-subspace (SHOULD: J basis higher).
3. KL is the J-weighted state error. To first order in a residual edit `δ` at layer m,
   `Δlogits ≈ W_U J δ`, so `KL(p_teacher ‖ p_student) ≈ ½ δᵀ (W_U J)ᵀ F (W_U J) δ`, where `F` is
   the output Fisher. Plain MSE on the 2048-d residual weights every direction equally, most of
   which the upper half ignores; KL weights directions by what they do downstream. This is why
   the decoder loss is KL and `relMSE(d_hat, d_true)` stays a diagnostic. It also answers the
   08-26 worry that "a small model can reduce MSE without learning a useful state".

J-steer (linear, unconditional, closed form) is the baseline the trained write must beat.

## 3. Data: RoomWorld

The Sparks-of-AGI Fig 5.8 task (`docs/sparks_of_agi_navigating_room_fig_5.8.png`) made causal: an
agent walks rooms in score notation, the model answers state questions and draws the map from z alone, and
replacing z with a second history changes the drawn map. `scripts/gen_roomworld.py`, pure templates, seed-stamped.

- House: 2x3 grid, six one-token room names, one object. Two arms walk the SAME house by
  different routes, so the pair shares vocabulary and differs only in state.
- Stored simulator lines use prose, but the model receives one score: `@office E @yard +coin W @office`.
  `@room` is the current room, cardinal letters are moves, `+/-object` are object actions, and `~noise`
  is irrelevant text. Histories have 8-15 events.
- Four question families, fixed question text per family, exact-match target:
  `where_you`, `where_obj`, `go_from_to` (route from here, bAbI qa19 form), and `map`. Map targets
  are compact edge scores such as `@office N @yard; @office E @study`; frozen Qwen gets F1 1.0
  on the canonical full-context gate for this edge format (job 42). Long causal demonstrations append
  one fixed completion footer after the parsed map. The footer is not a training target, contains no edge
  pattern, and does not affect map F1. -- PI
- Gate: keep a pair only if the frozen model with FULL context gets the first target token
  right on both arms (format-only for `go_from_to`). Then "z replaces context" is the claim, never
  "z beats a confused model".
- Each row stores the house, final position, observed edges, and per-line action/observation
  text, so the training script can simulate imagined moves and score them.
- Split by pair, so no house is in both train and validation.

## 4. Model

Frozen Qwen3-4B (36 layers, d = 2560), split at layer m = 18: `hidden_states[18]` is what layer 18
consumes. Lower = embeddings + layers 0..17, upper = layers 18..35 + norm + lm_head. Nothing in the
LLM trains; ~1M trainable params total, one full-context encode and a few decodes per step, so 4B
stays tractable. 4B not 1.7B because a ~2B model hardly holds an internal spatial map (and the
J-lens paper worked at larger scale). Latent width r = 64.

| module | map | init |
|---|---|---|
| `Read` | LSTM over `LN(W_r h_M)`, one r-wide state per score token | `W_r = V_rᵀ` from J̄ |
| `TransitionMemory` | at most 13 r-wide slots: learned source field, exact four-way action field, learned destination field | learned source/destination projections |
| `Step` | action identity restricts forward/reverse candidates; learned location matching retrieves a destination, then a GRUCell updates location | learned |
| `Write` | each answer token selects one slot field; hard map fields use categorical room/action/marker/semicolon logits, while other answers use learned residual Write | categorical fields have no learned output scale |
| `RoomHead` | shared linear room decoder for observed and imagined location z | learned |

Map decoding uses transition slots. Other question families use one final-room slot. Memory has fixed
capacity and an explicit mask; padded or zero memory produces exactly zero write. During imagination,
memory is unchanged and only location z advances. This is a learned operator over an extracted map
of observed transitions, not evidence for autonomous prediction of unseen edges. Exact parameter
counts print in `run.md`. -- PI

## 5. One training step

```python
# Full-context Qwen is the stopped teacher. The student sees the question/answer prefix without history.
h_M, h_final = frozen(score_history + question + target)
h_base = frozen(question + target)
d_true = h_final[target_columns] - h_base[target_columns]

z_tokens = Read(h_M)
for each observed move source --action--> destination:
    memory_slot = concat(W_source(z_source), one_hot(action), W_destination(z_destination))

# Each answer token selects source-room, action, destination-room, marker, or punctuation.
d_hat, field_bias = Write(memory, memory_mask, h_base, slot_index, token_role)
p = min(1, train_step / (0.60 * total_steps))
use_prediction = bernoulli(p)
d_train = where(use_prediction, d_hat, d_true)
student_logits = logits(h_base + d_train) + use_prediction * field_bias
L_hidden = relMSE(d_train, d_true)
L_decode = KL(logits(h_final).detach(), student_logits)
L_room = CE(RoomHead(z_observed), room)

# Stage two: Read and RoomHead freeze. TransitionMemory, Step, and Write train.
z_next = Step(z_source.detach(), action, memory, memory_mask)
L_dyn = MSE(z_next, z_destination.detach())
L_prior_room = CE(RoomHead(z_next), destination_room)

L_specific = relu(0.25 - (KL(wrong_memory) - KL(own_memory)) / stopgrad(KL(own_memory).clamp_min(0.1)))
stage1_loss = L_decode + L_hidden + L_room + L_specific
stage2_loss = L_decode + L_hidden + L_dyn + L_prior_room + L_specific
```

`field_bias` is a disclosed structured decoder. It is zero outside hard-routed map fields. Source and
destination room probabilities bias only the 12 one-token room logits; the exact action biases only
`N/E/S/W`; marker roles bias only their marker token; punctuation gets no bias. During generation and
token-accuracy evaluation, each hard field uses the selected memory probability itself as categorical
logits over its declared vocabulary. Its residual is zero, so neither a second residual decoder nor
frozen-Qwen room preferences can oppose the field. Semicolon is the sixth exact grammar role, so every completed edge advances one slot. After the last
valid slot, the same frozen-Qwen token loop emits the fixed completion footer under a single-token
output-grammar mask. Generic residual Write remains active for non-map answers. Soft field biases remain
only in the teacher KL path. -- PI

Why the curriculum (`p`), in wassname's words: "what if we smoothly drop out or sample more of the
true change? Then, to maintain a high score as the true change is removed, the model has to rely
more and more on z." Rising `kl` as `p` ramps is the design working.

`L_decode` and `L_dyn` are Dreamer's decoder and dynamics terms. Hidden relative MSE keeps the write
on the frozen residual manifold. Room cross-entropy reads the same location coordinate used by Step.
`L_specific` is the one satisfiable constraint: own memory must beat another real house's memory by
25%; it shuts off once satisfied. No representation loss or topology-classification loss is added.
Reverse cardinal moves train against the same observed transition slot. -- PI

Diagnostics logged every step, none of them in the loss: `kl_base` (no write), `kl_zero` (write
with z = 0), `kl_shuf` (write with another house's z), `kl_true` (d_true, the ceiling),
`relMSE(d_hat, d_true)`, `cos(d_hat, d_true)`, `‖d_hat‖/‖hs_turn‖`, `z_cos` across the pair,
`z_x` and `o_x` across houses (the collapse tells: ~1 means the posterior / the raw read carries
nothing house-specific), `z_last_cos` (cos of z with a posterior from only the last room; ~1 means
z is the current room, not the walk), grad norm per module. `kl_zero ≈ kl_write` means z is unused,
whatever the loss says; `kl_shuf ≈ kl_write` means whatever z carries is not the house.

## 6. Where the information flows

Figure: `docs/diagrams/lucid2_fletcher.png` (source `.typ` beside it) — the full grid, one column
per history line and per turn chunk, with each row's formula in the left margin. -- CLAUDE

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph frozen["frozen Qwen3-4B, one full-context pass"]
    IDS[lines ++ question ++ target] --> LOW[layers 0..17] --> HS[hs_full at layer 18]
    HS --> UPT[layers 18..35] --> LPT[teacher log probs]
  end
  HS -->|state at each line end| RD[read] --> O[o_1 .. o_N]
  O --> POST[post GRU] --> Z[z_N belief]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- imagination


def neighbors_seen(row: dict, cell: tuple[int, int]) -> list[tuple[str, tuple[int, int]]]:
    """Moves from cell along edges seen in this history, so imagination never needs an unseen map."""
    seen = true_edges(row)
    out = []
    for d, (dr, dc) in DIRS.items():
        nxt = (cell[0] + dr, cell[1] + dc)
        if nxt not in row["house"]:
            continue
        a, b = row["house"][cell], row["house"][nxt]
        e = (a, d, b) if a < b else (b, OPP[d], a)
        if e in seen:
            out.append((d, nxt))
    return out


def random_walk(row: dict, k: int, rng: random.Random) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    """k moves along seen edges from the final position. Returns action clauses and the room after each."""
    cell, actions, rooms = row["pos"], [], []
    for _ in range(k):
        opts = neighbors_seen(row, cell)
        if not opts:
            break
        d, cell = rng.choice(opts)
        actions.append(f"You go {d}.")
        rooms.append(row["house"][cell])
    return actions, rooms


@torch.no_grad()
def room_logprobs(mods: nn.ModuleDict, z: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    return mods["room"](z).log_softmax(-1)


@torch.no_grad()
def roll_actions(mods: nn.ModuleDict, z: Tensor, memory: Tensor,
                 memory_mask: Tensor, actions: list[str]) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor, list[dict]]:
    states, action_names, attentions = [], [], []
    memory_before = memory.clone()
    for action in actions:
        direction = action.removeprefix("You go ").removesuffix(".")
        action_id = torch.full((len(z),), list(DIRS).index(direction), device=z.device)
        z, attention = mods["step"](z, action_id, memory, memory_mask, return_weights=True)
        states.append(z.clone())
        action_names.append(action)
        attentions.append(attention)
    assert torch.equal(memory, memory_before)
    decoded = [room_logprobs(mods, state) for state in states]
    trace = [{"action": action, "decoded_room_index": int(lp[0].argmax()),
              "z_norm": float(state[0].norm()), "memory_unchanged": True,
              "top_memory_slot": int(attention[0].argmax()),
              "attention_entropy": float(-(attention[0] * attention[0].clamp_min(1e-9).log()).sum()),
              "transition": "memory-conditioned learned step",
              "qwen_rollout_calls": 0, "qwen_decode_calls": 0}
             for action, state, lp, attention in zip(action_names, states, decoded, attentions)]
    return z, decoded[-1], trace

def imagination_eval(mods: nn.ModuleDict, model: nn.Module, rows: list[dict], cfg: Cfg, pad_id: int, eos_id: int,
                     room_names: list[str], room_ids: Tensor, rng: random.Random, log: RunLog, tag: str, quote: bool) -> dict:
    eval_rng = random.Random(cfg.seed + 2026)  # identical cases at init, mid, post, and restored final
    probe_rows = []
    for row in rows:
        current = row["house"][row["pos"]]
        probe_rows.append(row | chat_encode_row(_TOKENIZER, row["lines"], WHERE_Q, " " + current + "."))
    z0, memory, memory_mask = planning_state_of(mods, model, probe_rows, cfg, pad_id)
    acc = {}
    for k in range(1, cfg.imag_k + 1):
        hits = n = 0
        for r_i, r in enumerate(rows):
            actions, rooms = random_walk(r, k, eval_rng)
            if len(actions) < k:
                continue
            expect = rooms[-1] if k else r["house"][r["pos"]]
            _, lp, trace = roll_actions(mods, z0[r_i:r_i + 1].clone(),
                                        memory[r_i:r_i + 1], memory_mask[r_i:r_i + 1], actions)
            pred = room_names[int(lp.argmax())]
            hits += pred == expect
            n += 1
            if quote and r_i == 0:
                here = r["house"][r["pos"]]
                plan = [here] + rooms if k else None
                kw = dict(house=r["house"], path=path_rooms(r["lines"]), here=here, plan=plan)
                log.text(f"## imagination -> {tag} -> k={k}: actions {actions} expect `{expect}` decode `{pred}` "
                         f"qwen_block_calls=0 (pair {r['pair_id']} {r['walk']})\n\ntrace: `{trace}`\n\n"
                         + "\n".join(edges_ascii(true_edges(r), f"k={k} (`*` now, `...` been, `~~~` plan):", **kw)))
        acc[k] = {"imag_acc": hits / max(n, 1), "n": n, "qwen_block_calls": 0}

    plan_hits = plan_n = plan_chance = 0.0
    for r_i, r in enumerate(rows):
        plans = [([f"You go {d1}.", f"You go {d2}."], c2)
                 for d1, c1 in neighbors_seen(r, r["pos"]) for d2, c2 in neighbors_seen(r, c1)]
        if len(plans) < 2:
            continue
        goal_cell = eval_rng.choice(sorted(set(c for _, c in plans)))
        goal = room_names.index(r["house"][goal_cell])
        scores = [float(roll_actions(mods, z0[r_i:r_i + 1].clone(),
                                     memory[r_i:r_i + 1], memory_mask[r_i:r_i + 1], acts)[1][0, goal])
                  for acts, _ in plans]
        pick = int(torch.tensor(scores).argmax())
        plan_hits += plans[pick][1] == goal_cell
        plan_chance += sum(c == goal_cell for _, c in plans) / len(plans)
        if quote and plan_n == 0:
            rows_p = [{"plan": " ".join(a), "reaches": r["house"][c], "logp(goal)": f"{s:+.3f}",
                       "chosen": "<-" * (j == pick), "goal": "<-" * (c == goal_cell)}
                      for j, ((a, c), s) in enumerate(zip(plans, scores))]
            log.text(f"## imagination -> {tag} -> planning long form (pair {r['pair_id']} {r['walk']}): "
                     f"goal `{r['house'][goal_cell]}` from `{r['house'][r['pos']]}`; qwen_block_calls=0\n\n" + table(rows_p))
        plan_n += 1
    res = {"acc": acc, "plan_acc": plan_hits / max(plan_n, 1), "plan_hits": plan_hits,
           "plan_chance": plan_chance / max(plan_n, 1), "plan_n": plan_n,
           "chance": 1 / len(room_names), "qwen_block_calls": 0, "memory_unchanged": True}
    log.text(f"## imagination -> {tag}\n\n" + table([{"k": k, **v} for k, v in acc.items()])
             + f"\n\nplan_acc {res['plan_acc']:.2f} vs chance {res['plan_chance']:.2f} (n={plan_n}); "
               "SHOULD: imag_acc remains above room chance beyond k=1 and plan_acc beats plan_chance.")
    log.event("imagination", {"tag": tag, **res})
    return res

## Introduction

Reinforcement learning has enabled computers to solve tasks through interaction, such as surpassing humans in the games of Go and Dota [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib1), [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib2). It is also a key component for improving large language models beyond what is demonstrated in their pretraining data[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib3), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib4). While PPO [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5) has become a standard algorithm in the field of reinforcement learning, more specialized algorithms are often employed to achieve higher performance. These specialized algorithms target the unique challenges posed by different application domains, such as continuous control [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib6), discrete actions [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), sparse rewards [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib9), image inputs [10](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib10), spatial environments [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib11), and board games [12](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib12). However, applying reinforcement learning algorithms to sufficiently new tasks—such as moving from video games to robotics tasks—requires substantial effort, expertise, and computational resources for tweaking the hyperparameters of the algorithm [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib13). This brittleness poses a bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to new problems and also limits the applicability of reinforcement learning to computationally expensive models or tasks where tuning is prohibitive. Creating a general algorithm that learns to master new domains without having to be reconfigured has been a central challenge in artificial intelligence and would open up reinforcement learning to a wide range of practical applications.

We present Dreamer, a general algorithm that outperforms specialized expert algorithms across a wide range of domains while using fixed hyperparameters, making reinforcement learning readily applicable to new problems. The algorithm is based on the idea of learning a world model that equips the agent with rich perception and the ability to imagine the future[14](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib14), [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib15), [16](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib16). The world model predicts the outcomes of potential actions, a critic neural network judges the value of each outcome, and an actor neural network chooses actions to reach the best outcomes. Although intuitively appealing, robustly learning and leveraging world models to achieve strong task performance has been an open problem[17](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib17). Dreamer overcomes this challenge through a range of robustness techniques based on normalization, balancing, and transformations. We observe robust learning not only across over 150 tasks from the domains summarized in [Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), but also across model sizes and training budgets, offering a predictable way to increase performance. Notably, larger model sizes not only achieve higher scores but also require less interaction to solve a task.

To push the boundaries of reinforcement learning, we consider the popular video game Minecraft that has become a focal point of research in recent years [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20), with international competitions held for developing algorithms that autonomously learn to collect diamonds in Minecraft 1 1 1 The MineRL Diamond Competitions were held in 2019, 2020, and 2021 and provided a dataset of human expert trajectories: [https://minerl.io/diamond](https://minerl.io/diamond). Competitions in the following years focused on a wide range of tasks.. Solving this problem without human data has been widely recognized as a substantial challenge for artificial intelligence because of the sparse rewards, exploration difficulty, long time horizons, and the procedural diversity of this open world game [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18). Due to these obstacles, previous approaches resorted to using human expert data and domain-specific curricula [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). Applied out of the box, Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.

## Learning algorithm

We present the third generation of the Dreamer algorithm[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib21), [22](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib22). The algorithm consists of three neural networks: the world model predicts the outcomes of potential actions, the critic judges the value of each outcome, and the actor chooses actions to reach the most valuable outcomes. The components are trained concurrently from replayed experience while the agent interacts with the environment. To succeed across domains, all three components need to accommodate different signal magnitudes and robustly balance terms in their objectives. This is challenging as we are not only targeting similar tasks within the same domain but aim to learn across diverse domains with fixed hyperparameters. This section introduces the world model, critic, and actor along with their robust loss functions, as well as tools for robustly predicting quantities of unknown orders of magnitude.

### World model learning

The world model learns compact representations of sensory inputs through autoencoding [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib23) and enables planning by predicting future representations and rewards for potential actions. We implement the world model as a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) [24](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib24), shown in [Figure 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Introduction ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"). First, an encoder maps sensory inputs x_{t} to stochastic representations z_{t}. Then, a sequence model with recurrent state h_{t} predicts the sequence of these representations given past actions a_{t-1}. The concatenation of h_{t} and z_{t} forms the model state from which we predict rewards r_{t} and episode continuation flags c_{t}\in\{0,1\} and reconstruct the inputs to ensure informative representations:

Complex 3D environments contain details unnecessary for control and thus prompt a stronger regularizer to simplify the representations and make them more predictable. In games with static backgrounds and where individual pixels may matter for the task, a weak regularizer is required to extract fine details. We find that combining free bits with a small representation loss resolves this dilemma, allowing for fixed hyperparameters across domains. ### Critic learning

The actor and critic neural networks learn behaviors purely from abstract trajectories of representations predicted by the world model [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib14). For environment interaction, we select actions by sampling from the actor network without lookahead planning. The actor and critic operate on model states s_{t}\doteq\{h_{t},z_{t}\} and thus benefit from the Markovian representations learned by the recurrent world model. The actor aims to maximize the return R_{t}\doteq\textstyle\sum_{\tau=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau}r_{t+\tau} with a discount factor \gamma=0.997 for each model state. To consider rewards beyond the prediction horizon T=16, the critic learns to approximate the distribution of returns [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib28) for each state under the current actor behavior:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\text{Actor:}\quad&&a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}%
\;|\;s_{t})\qquad&\text{Critic:}\quad&&v_{\psi}(R_{t}\;|\;s_{t})\end{aligned}(4)

Starting from representations of replayed inputs, the world model and actor generate a trajectory of imagined model states s_{1:T}, actions a_{1:T}, rewards r_{1:T}, and continuation flags c_{1:T}. Because the critic predicts a distribution, we read out its predicted values v_{t}\doteq\operatorname{E}[v_{\psi}(\,\cdot\;|\;s_{t})] as the expectation of the distribution. To estimate returns that consider rewards beyond the prediction horizon, we compute bootstrapped \lambda-returns [29](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib29) that integrate the predicted rewards and the values. The critic learns to predict the distribution of the return estimates R^{\lambda}_{t} using the maximum likelihood loss:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\psi)\doteq-\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}%
\ln p_{\psi}(R^{\lambda}_{t}\;|\;s_{t})\qquad R^{\lambda}_{t}\doteq r_{t}+%
\gamma c_{t}\Big{(}(1-\lambda)v_{t}+\lambda R^{\lambda}_{t+1}\Big{)}\qquad R^{%
\lambda}_{T}\doteq v_{T}\end{aligned}(5)

While a simple choice would be to parameterize the critic as a Normal distribution, the return distribution can have multiple modes and vary by orders of magnitude across environments. To stabilize and accelerate learning under these conditions, we parameterize the critic as categorical distribution with exponentially spaced bins, decoupling the scale of gradients from the prediction targets as described later. To improve value prediction in environments where rewards are challenging to predict, we apply the critic loss both to imagined trajectories with loss scale \beta_{\mathrm{val}}=1 and to trajectories sampled from the replay buffer with loss scale \beta_{\mathrm{repval}}=0.3. The critic replay loss uses the imagination returns R^{\lambda}_{t} at the start states of the imagination rollouts as on-policy value annotations for the replay trajectory to then compute \lambda-returns over the replay rewards.

Because the critic regresses targets that depend on its own predictions, we stabilize learning by regularizing the critic towards predicting the outputs of an exponentially moving average of its own parameters. This is similar to target networks used previously in reinforcement learning [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7) but allows us to compute returns using the current critic network. We further noticed that the randomly initialized reward predictor and critic networks at the start of training can result in large predicted rewards that can delay the onset of learning. We thus initialize the output weight matrix of the reward predictor and critic to zeros, which alleviates the problem and accelerates early learning.

### Actor learning

The actor learns to choose actions that maximize return while exploring through an entropy regularizer [30](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib30). However, the correct scale for this regularizer depends both on the scale and frequency of rewards in the environment. Ideally, we would like the agent to explore more if rewards are sparse and exploit more if rewards are dense or nearby. At the same time, the exploration amount should not be influenced by arbitrary scaling of rewards in the environment. This requires normalizing the return scale while preserving information about reward frequency.

To use a fixed entropy scale of \eta=3\times 10^{-4} across domains, we normalize returns to be approximately contained in the interval [0,1]. In practice, substracting an offset from the returns does not change the actor gradient and thus dividing by the range S is sufficient. Moreover, to avoid amplifying noise from function approximation under sparse rewards, we only scale down large return magnitudes but leave small returns below the threshold of L=1 untouched. We use the Reinforce estimator [31](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib31) for both discrete and continuous actions, resulting in the surrogate loss function:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta)\doteq-\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T%
}\operatorname{sg}\!\Big{(}\big{(}R^{\lambda}_{t}-v_{\psi}(s_{t})\big{)}/\max(%
1,\,S)\Big{)}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\;|\;s_{t})+\,\eta\operatorname{H}\big{[}%
\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\;\big{|}\;s_{t})\big{]}\end{aligned}(6)

The return distribution can be multi-modal and include outliers, especially for randomized environments where some episodes have higher achievable returns than others. Normalizing by the smallest and largest observed returns would then scale returns down too much and may cause suboptimal convergence. To be robust to these outliers, we compute the range from the 5 th to the 95 th return percentile over the return batch and smooth out the estimate using an exponential moving average:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} S\doteq\operatorname{EMA}\!\big{(}\operatorname{%
Per}(R^{\lambda}_{t},95)-\operatorname{Per}(R^{\lambda}_{t},5),0.99\big{)}\end%
{aligned}(7)

Previous work typically normalizes advantages[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5) rather than returns, which puts a fixed amount of emphasis on maximizing returns over entropy regardless of whether rewards are within reach. Scaling up advantages when rewards are sparse can amplify noise that outweighs the entropy regularizer and stagnates exploration. Normalizing rewards or returns by standard deviation can fail under sparse rewards where their standard deviation is near zero, drastically amplifying rewards regardless of their size. Constrained optimization targets a fixed entropy on average across states [32](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib32), [33](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib33) regardless of achievable returns, which is robust but explores slowly under sparse rewards and converges lower under dense rewards. We did not find stable hyperparameters across domains for these approaches. Return normalization with a denominator limit overcomes these challenges, exploring rapidly under sparse rewards and converging to high performance across diverse domains.

### Robust predictions

Reconstructing inputs and predicting rewards and returns can be challenging because the scale of these quantities can vary across domains. Predicting large targets using a squared loss can lead to divergence whereas absolute and Huber losses [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7) stagnate learning. On the other hand, normalizing targets based on running statistics [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5) introduces non-stationarity into the optimization. We suggest the symlog squared error as a simple solution to this dilemma. For this, a neural network f(x,\theta) with inputs x and parameters \theta learns to predict a transformed version of its targets y. To read out predictions \hat{y} of the network, we apply the inverse transformation:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L(\theta)}\doteq\textstyle\frac{1}{2}%
\big{(}f(x,\theta)-\operatorname{symlog}(y)\big{)}^{2}\qquad\hat{y}\doteq%
\operatorname{symexp}\!\big{(}f(x,\theta)\big{)}\end{aligned}(8)

Using the logarithm as transformation would not allow us to predict targets that take on negative values. Therefore, we choose a function from the bi-symmetric logarithmic family [34](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib34) that we name symlog as the transformation with the symexp function as its inverse:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \operatorname{symlog}(x)\doteq\operatorname{sign}%
(x)\ln\!\big{(}|x|+1\big{)}\qquad\operatorname{symexp}(x)\doteq\operatorname{%
sign}(x)\big{(}\!\exp(|x|)-1\big{)}\end{aligned}(9)

The symlog function compresses the magnitudes of both large positive and negative values. Unlike the logarithm, it is symmetric around the origin while preserving the input sign. This allows the optimization process to quickly move the network predictions to large values when needed. The symlog function approximates the identity around the origin so that it does not affect learning of targets that are already small enough.

For potentially stochastic targets, such as rewards or returns, we introduce the symexp twohot loss. Here, the network outputs the logits for a softmax distribution over exponentially spaced bins b_{i}\in B. Predictions are read out as the weighted average of the bin positions weighted by their predicted probabilities. Importantly, the network can output any continuous value in the interval because the weighted average can fall between the buckets:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \hat{y}\doteq\operatorname{softmax}(f(x))^{T}B%
\qquad B\doteq\operatorname{symexp}(\begin{bmatrix}-20&...&+20\end{bmatrix})%
\end{aligned}(10)

The network is trained on twohot encoded targets [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib28), a generalization of onehot encoding to continuous values. The twohot encoding of a scalar is a vector with |B| entries that are all 0 except at the indices k and k+1 of the two bins closest to the encoded scalar. The two entries sum up to 1, with linearly higher weight given to the bin that is closer to the encoded continuous number. The network is then trained to minimize the categorical cross entropy loss for classification with soft targets. Note that the loss only depends on the probabilities assigned to the bins but not on the continuous values associated with the bin locations, decoupling the size of the gradients from the size of the targets:

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\theta)\doteq-\operatorname{twohot}(y%
)^{T}\operatorname{log\,softmax}(f(x,\theta))\end{aligned}(11)

Applying these principles, Dreamer transforms vector observations using the symlog functions, both for the encoder inputs and the decoder targets and employs the synexp twohot loss for the reward predictor and critic. We find that these techniques enable robust and fast learning across many diverse domains. For critic learning, an alternative asymmetric transformation has previously been proposed [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib35), which we found less effective on average across domains. Unlike alternatives, symlog transformations avoid truncating large targets [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), introducing non-stationary from normalization [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5), or adjusting network weights when new extreme values are detected [36](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib36).

## Results

We evaluate the generality of Dreamer across 8 domains—with over 150 tasks—under fixed hyperparameters. We designed the experiments to compare Dreamer to the best methods in the literature, which are often specifically designed and tuned for the benchmark at hand. We further compare to a high-quality implementation of PPO[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5), a standard reinforcement learning algorithm that is known for its robustness. We run PPO with fixed hyperparameters chosen to maximize performance across domains and that reproduce strong published results of PPO on ProcGen[37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). To push the boundaries of reinforcement learning, we apply Dreamer to the challenging video game Minecraft, comparing it to strong previous algorithms. Finally, we analyze the importance of individual components of Dreamer and its robustness to different model sizes and computational budgets. All Dreamer agents are trained on a single Nvidia A100 GPU each, making it reproducible for many research labs. A public implementation of Dreamer that reproduces all results is available on the project website.

#### Benchmarks

We perform an extensive empirical study across 8 domains that include continuous and discrete actions, visual and low-dimensional inputs, dense and sparse rewards, different reward scales, 2D and 3D worlds, and procedural generation. [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") summarizes the benchmark results, showing that Dreamer outperforms a wide range of previous expert algorithms across diverse domains. Crucially, Dreamer substantially outperforms PPO across all domains.

*   •Atari This established benchmark contains 57 Atari 2600 games with a budget of 200M frames, posing a diverse range of challenges[38](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib38). We use the sticky action simulator setting [39](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib39). Dreamer outperforms the powerful MuZero algorithm[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8) while using only a fraction of the computational resources. Dreamer also outperforms the widely-used expert algorithms Rainbow [40](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib40) and IQN [41](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib41). 
*   •ProcGen This benchmark of 16 games features randomized levels and visual distractions to test the robustness and generalization of agents[42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42). Within the budget of 50M frames, Dreamer matches the tuned expert algorithm PPG [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37) and outperforms Rainbow[42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42), [40](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib40). Our PPO agent with fixed hyperparameters matches the published score of the highly tuned official PPO implementation[37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). 
*   •DMLab This suite of 30 tasks features 3D environments that test spatial and temporal reasoning [43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). In 100M frames, Dreamer exceeds the performance of the scalable IMPALA and R2D2+ agents [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib35) at 1B environment steps, amounting to a data-efficiency gain of over 1000%. We note that these baselines were not designed for data-efficiency but serve as a valuable comparison point for the performance previously achievable at scale. 
*   •Atari100k This data-efficiency benchmark comntains 26 Atari games and a budget of only 400K frames, amounting to 2 hours of game time [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib17). EfficientZero [44](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib44) holds the state-of-the-art by combining online tree search, prioritized replay, and hyperparameter scheduling, but also resets levels early to increase data diversity, making a comparison difficult. Without this complexity, Dreamer outperforms the best remaining methods, including the transformer-based IRIS and TWM agents, the model-free SPR, and SimPLe [45](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib45). 
*   •Proprio Control This benchmark contains 18 control tasks with continuous actions, proprioceptive vector inputs, and a budget of 500K environment steps [46](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib46). The tasks range from classical control over locomotion to robot manipulation tasks, featuring dense and sparse rewards. Dreamer sets a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming D4PG, DMPO, and MPO [33](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib33). 
*   •Visual Control This benchmark consists of 20 continuous control tasks where the agent receives only high-dimensional images as input and has a budget of 1M environment steps [46](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib46). Dreamer establishes a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming DrQ-v2 and CURL [47](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib47), which are specialized to visual environments and leverage data augmentation. 
*   •BSuite This benchmark includes 23 environments with a total of 468 configurations that are specifically designed to test credit assignment, robustness to reward scale and stochasticity, memory, generalization, and exploration [48](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib48). Dreamer establishes a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming Boot DQN and other methods [49](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib49). Dreamer improves over previous algorithms especially in the scale robustness category. 

#### Minecraft

Collecting diamonds in the popular game Minecraft has been a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence[18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). Every episode in this game is set in a unique randomly generated and infinite 3D world. Episodes last until the player dies or up to 36000 steps equaling 30 minutes, during which the player needs to discover a sequence of 12 items from sparse rewards by foraging for resources and crafting tools. It takes about 20 minutes for experienced human players to obtain diamonds[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). We follow the block breaking setting of prior work [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19) because the provided action space would make it challenging for stochastic policies to keep a key pressed for a prolonged time.

Because of the training time in this complex domain, extensive tuning would be difficult for Minecraft. Instead, we apply Dreamer out of the box with its default hyperparameters. As shown in [Figures 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") and[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without using human data as was required by VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) or adaptive curricula[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19). All the Dreamer agents we trained on Minecraft discover diamonds in 100M environment steps. While several strong baselines progress to advanced items such as the iron pickaxe, none of them discovers a diamond.

#### Ablations

In [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), we ablate the robustness techniques and learning signals on a diverse set of 14 tasks to understand their importance. The training curves of individual tasks are included in the supplementary material. We observe that all robustness techniques contribute to performance, most notably the KL objective of the world model, followed by return normalization and symexp twohot regression for reward and value prediction. In general, we find that each individual technique is critical on a subset of tasks but may not affect performance on other tasks.

To investigate the effect of the world model, we ablate the learning signals of Dreamer by stopping either the task-specific reward and value prediction gradients or the task-agnostic reconstruction gradients from shaping its representations. Unlike previous reinforcement learning algorithms that often rely only on task-specific learning signals[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), Dreamer rests predominantly on the unsupervised objective of its world model. This finding could allow for future algorithm variants that leverage pretraining on unsupervised data.

#### Scaling properties

To investigate whether Dreamer can scale robustly, we train 6 model sizes ranging from 12M to 400M parameters, as well as different replay ratios on Crafter [50](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib50) and a DMLab task[43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). The replay ratio affects the number of gradient updates performed by the agent. [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") shows robust learning with fixed hyperparameters across the compared model sizes and replay ratios. Moreover, increasing the model size directly translates to both higher task performance and a lower data requirement. Increasing the number of gradient steps further reduces the interactions needed to learn successful behaviors. The results show that Dreamer learns robustly across model sizes and replay ratios and that its performance and provides a predictable way for increasing performance given computational resources.

# 4. Experiments 

We perform a wide range of experiments to evaluate and explore the capabilities of Dreamer 4. The majority of our experiments focus on Minecraft, a complex video game that features infinite open worlds including monsters and hundreds of items that can be mined or crafted, with raw pixel observations and low-level mouse and keyboard actions. We primarily use the VPT dataset 15 that contains 2541 hours of contractor gameplay with 360p video and mouse and keyboard actions at 20 FPS. The experiments are designed to answer the following questions: • Does Dreamer 4 learn to solve challenging control tasks purely by imagination training inside the world model, without online environment interaction? (Section 4.1) • How well does Dreamer 4 learn to predict accurate object interactions and game mechanics in Minecraft compared to previous world models? (Section 4.2) • How much action data does Dreamer 4 need for learning action conditioning, and how far does the learned action grounding generalize? (Section 4.3) • To what extent does each component of its objective and architecture contribute to the perfor-mance of Dreamer 4? (Section 4.4) We train models with 2B parameters—400M for the tokenizer and 1.6B for the dynamics model—on 256 to 1024 TPU-v5p with batch size 1 per device and FSDP sharding 44,45 . To improve generations without context, we treat 30% of the videos in the batch as separate images, effectively training the dynamics model to generate start frames. For Minecraft, we use 256 spatial tokens with 192 frames context length and 256 batch length. For the real world datasets, we use 512 spatial tokens with 96 frames context length and 128 batch length.

4.1. Offline Diamond Challenge 

We evaluate Dreamer 4 on the Minecraft diamond challenge, a long-horizon control task that re-quires solving several sub tasks, such as gathering materials and crafting tools in a complex proce-durally generated 3D world from raw pixels and mouse and keyboard actions. Human players with Minecraft experience take 20 minutes to collect a diamond on average, corresponding to sequences of 24,000 mouse and keyboard actions. 

Offline setting While previous agents have achieved diamonds in Minecraft through online inter-action with the environment 1,15 , deploying partially-trained policies is often infeasible for practical applications, such as physical robots, because ensuring safety, resetting the scene, and providing rewards in real time is difficult. Instead, we focus on the challenge of learning purely offline from a fixed experience dataset. We only use the VPT contractor dataset 15 —which contains 2.5K hours of videos, actions, and event annotations—without allowing the agent to interact with the environ-ment for learning, and compare to baselines in this offline setting. We follow the VPT evaluation protocol of raw pixel inputs and low-level mouse and keyboard actions, requiring crafting through the in-game user interface. Episodes last 60 minutes, starting from an empty inventory in randomly generated Minecraft worlds. 

Implementation Dreamer 4 learns a single transformer that predicts inputs, actions, rewards, and values. To build a steerable agent, we opt for a multi-task setting and condition the actions, re-wards, and values on task embeddings. We annotate the tasks and their sparse binary rewards using the existing events in the VPT dataset. Table 4 lists the 20 tasks and Table 6 shows the linear prompt sequence that guides the agent to reach diamonds during evaluation in the environment. To amplify the signal in the dataset during behavior cloning, reward modeling, and reinforcement learning, we use data mixture of 50% uniform sequences and 50% relevant sequences that accomplish one of the tasks. The behavioral cloning loss is applied only on the relevant fraction, while the dynamics loss is applied only on the uniform sequences to avoid optimistic generations. We use one-hot task indicators but text embeddings could easily be used. We represent keyboard actions as 23 binary distributions and mouse actions as a categorical with 121 classes using foveated discretization 15 .

4.3. Action Generalization 

One promise of world models is to leverage diverse unlabeled videos to teach agents about the world. For example, a world model could learn general physics and object interactions from web videos where actions are not available. In this section, we investigate the amount of paired videos with actions that are needed for grounding an embodiment into the Dreamer 4 world model. Intuitively, the world model has to learn a broader distribution of possible outcomes when actions are missing, and can narrow the distribution down when actions are provided. Moreover, we investigate how well the action conditioning generalizes, not just within the same distribution, but also out of distribution to parts of the world specifically held out. To measure the accuracy of the action conditioning, we compare action-conditioned multi-step generations to ground truth videos on the holdout set. We report PSNR and SSIM for 16-step generations given 320 frames of context. 

Amount of actions To understand the amount of video with actions needed to learn action con-ditioning, we train Dreamer 4 on all 2541 hours of videos in the VPT dataset, but only provide actions for a small subset of the videos. When actions are unavailable, the dynamics model is con-ditioned on a learned embedding, as described in Section 3.2. We train Dreamer 4 models with 0, 10, 100, 1000, and 2541 hours of actions. The available actions are the first in sequential order of the dataset, corresponding to fewer unique worlds and players than random shuffling would yield. Figure 7 show the quality of the action conditioning compared to training with no actions at all to training with all actions. With only 10 hours of actions, Dreamer 4 achieves 53% PSNR and 75% SSIM compared to a model trained with all actions. With 100 hours of actions, the performance increases further to 85% PSNR and 100% SSIM. This result demonstrates that world models absorb the majority of their knowledge from unlabeled videos, and require only a small amount of actions. 

Action extrapolation In principle, world models may not only learn action ground from a few actions but also generalize their action conditioning to completely new scenarios. In the future, this could allow world models to absorb general knowledge from diverse web videos to simulate agents in diverse environments. We target 20 FPS interactive inference on a single H100 GPU, matching the tick rate of Minecraft and the framerate of the VPT dataset. With 64 sampling steps per frame, the baseline falls short of real-time generations with only 0.8 FPS on one H100 GPU, while 4 sampling steps achieve 9.1 FPS but result in poor quality. Shortcut models 21 nearly recover the original visual quality with only 4 sampling steps. We then parameterize the model to make x-space predic-tions, compute the loss in x-space, and apply the ramp loss weight. These changes substantially improve generation quality over traditional v-space prediction, especially for long generations. We hypothesize that the prediction tar-gets in x-space are more structured and thus reduce the risk of high-frequency errors that accumulate over time. Figure 8 compares the visual quality of shortcut forcing to diffusion forcing—both using the x-space loss with ramp weight—for a wider range of sampling steps. Training on alternating batch lengths is similar to progressive training and speeds up learning while allowing to generate long videos for inspection throughout training. Using temporal attention only every 4 layers not only speeds up training and inference 39 but also improves generation quality, possibly because of the inductive bias of spatial attention that focuses computation on the current frame. GQA further accelerates generations without degrading performance. Switching the long context layers from dense to time-only attention accelerates inference at a mild quality cost, and prepares us to increase the overall number of tokens subsequently. While the register tokens do not improve FVD measurably, we qualitatively notice that they improve temporal consistency. After these changes, training and inference is fast enough to increase model capacity through more spatial tokens, improving predictions of complex interactions. The complete model achieves an FVD of 57 compared to 306 for the naive diffusion forcing transformer baseline and 124 for the complete architecture with v-space prediction and losses.

Table 3: Comparison of experimental setups for different Minecraft agents. Dreamer 4 learns purely from offline experience and requires 100 × less data than previous keyboard and mouse agents. See Figure 10 for examples of input images. 

> 16

# 5. Related Work 

Minecraft agents Obtaining diamonds in the video game Minecraft has been a focus of intelligent agent research 51–54 , a long-horizon task that requires gathering resources and crafting tools through thousands of low-level actions in complex procedurally generated 3D worlds. Different setups have been used in the literature, with Table 3 summarizing the ones relevant to our work. VPT 15 collects 2.5K hours of contractor gameplay and uses it to annotate 270K hours of web videos with synthetic mouse and keyboard actions. Behavioral cloning on this large offline dataset and targeted finetuning on “early-game” data yields a policy that occasionally obtains wooden pickaxes. Following up with 194K hours of online reinforcement learning results in a policy that obtains diamonds and diamond pickaxes. Dreamer 3 1 learns to collect diamonds from scratch from 1.4K hours of online interaction, without any human data. It uses the MineRL competition action space that includes abstract crafting actions. Other works have explored novel algorithms for easier tasks 55–58 . In this paper, we train an agent to achieve diamonds purely from the 2.5K hour contractor dataset, without any online interaction. We use low-level mouse and keyboard actions and high-resolution image inputs. 

World model agents Learning behaviors based on learned models of the environment has been explored for a long time 59–61 . Visual Foresight 62 , the work by Ha and Schmidhuber 63 , and PlaNet 64 

achieved world models accurate enough for planning from pixels. With Dreamer, world models have become the state-of-the-art approach for solving control problems with high-dimensional inputs, out-performing model-free reinforcement learning in robustness, efficiency, and final performance 1,65,66 .World models based on transformers or diffusion objectives have demonstrated high data efficiency for discrete control 67–69 . However, these world models have been limited in model capacity, restrict-ing their applicability to relatively simple simulated environments. 

Scalable world models Larger world models have been shown to simulate more complex data distributions 70 . World models like Genie 3 generate highly diverse scenes and simulate camera movement and simple interactions 7,9,10,12 . PlayerOne 8 and PEVA 11 condition on more detailed hu-man movement. Oasis 46 , Lucid 47 , and MineWorld 48 learn Minecraft simulators from mouse and keyboard inputs. Whereas Oasis captures simple game mechanics and achieves real-time inference on specialized hardware, Lucid’s predictions diverge quickly and MineWorld is slower than real time. GameNGen 71 finetunes Stable Diffusion into a playable simulator of a level of the game Doom. DIA-MOND 4 learns a simulator of a level of the game CS GO, achieving short-term predictions. GAIA 72,73 

generates driving scenarios from real world data. However, these world models still struggle to pre-dict complex object interactions precisely enough for imagination training. 

Fast generation Enabling fast and accurate generations has been a long-standing challenge in generating modeling. MaskGit generates discrete tokens in parallel to accelerate sampling over au-toregressive models 74 . Diffusion models are often distilled to enable sampling using fewer forward passes 75,76 , which requires two training phases. Consistency models learn straight paths to en-able fast image generation but require careful schedules 77–79 , with successful applications to video generation 80 . Shortcut models 21 condition flows on both noise level and step size, producing fast generative models in one training phase and without schedules. Mean Flow 81 extends the idea of conditioning on the step size to a continuous time formulation. Efficient and sparse architectures are used for video generation because of the large number of tokens 38,82,83 . These models do not support interactive inference and many of the techniques are complimentary to our work. 

> 17

# 6. Discussion 

We present Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve challenging control tasks by imagination training inside of a fast and accurate world model. Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without online interaction. This achievement demonstrates its learning successful long-horizon strategies in complex environments. Learning purely from offline datasets enables applications where online interaction is impractical or unsafe. The world model of Dreamer 4 rests on a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture to predict complex object interactions while supporting interactive inference in real time on a single GPU. We demonstrate that it significantly outperforms previous world models on Minecraft, where it accurately predicts a wide range of game mechanics from mouse and keyboard inputs. However, the world model is far from a full clone of the game, especially due to short memory and imprecise inventory predictions, leaving Minecraft as an ideal benchmark for future world model and agent research. We also show that Dreamer 4 learns accurate action conditioning from only a small amount of videos with actions, allowing it to absorb the majority of its knowledge from diverse unlabeled videos. Promising future directions include pretraining on general internet videos, integrating long-term memory into the world model and agent, incorporating language understanding, leveraging small amounts of corrective online data, and automatically discovering goals to break up long tasks. Dreamer 4 offers a reliable and performant starting point for these explorations.
