## Results

We evaluate the generality of Dreamer across 8 domains—with over 150 tasks—under fixed hyperparameters. We designed the experiments to compare Dreamer to the best methods in the literature, which are often specifically designed and tuned for the benchmark at hand. We further compare to a high-quality implementation of PPO[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib5), a standard reinforcement learning algorithm that is known for its robustness. We run PPO with fixed hyperparameters chosen to maximize performance across domains and that reproduce strong published results of PPO on ProcGen[37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). To push the boundaries of reinforcement learning, we apply Dreamer to the challenging video game Minecraft, comparing it to strong previous algorithms. Finally, we analyze the importance of individual components of Dreamer and its robustness to different model sizes and computational budgets. All Dreamer agents are trained on a single Nvidia A100 GPU each, making it reproducible for many research labs. A public implementation of Dreamer that reproduces all results is available on the project website.

#### Benchmarks

We perform an extensive empirical study across 8 domains that include continuous and discrete actions, visual and low-dimensional inputs, dense and sparse rewards, different reward scales, 2D and 3D worlds, and procedural generation. [Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") summarizes the benchmark results, showing that Dreamer outperforms a wide range of previous expert algorithms across diverse domains. Crucially, Dreamer substantially outperforms PPO across all domains.

*   •Atari This established benchmark contains 57 Atari 2600 games with a budget of 200M frames, posing a diverse range of challenges[38](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib38). We use the sticky action simulator setting [39](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib39). Dreamer outperforms the powerful MuZero algorithm[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8) while using only a fraction of the computational resources. Dreamer also outperforms the widely-used expert algorithms Rainbow [40](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib40) and IQN [41](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib41). 
*   •ProcGen This benchmark of 16 games features randomized levels and visual distractions to test the robustness and generalization of agents[42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42). Within the budget of 50M frames, Dreamer matches the tuned expert algorithm PPG [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37) and outperforms Rainbow[42](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib42), [40](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib40). Our PPO agent with fixed hyperparameters matches the published score of the highly tuned official PPO implementation[37](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib37). 
*   •DMLab This suite of 30 tasks features 3D environments that test spatial and temporal reasoning [43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). In 100M frames, Dreamer exceeds the performance of the scalable IMPALA and R2D2+ agents [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib35) at 1B environment steps, amounting to a data-efficiency gain of over 1000%. We note that these baselines were not designed for data-efficiency but serve as a valuable comparison point for the performance previously achievable at scale. 
*   •Atari100k This data-efficiency benchmark comntains 26 Atari games and a budget of only 400K frames, amounting to 2 hours of game time [17](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib17). EfficientZero [44](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib44) holds the state-of-the-art by combining online tree search, prioritized replay, and hyperparameter scheduling, but also resets levels early to increase data diversity, making a comparison difficult. Without this complexity, Dreamer outperforms the best remaining methods, including the transformer-based IRIS and TWM agents, the model-free SPR, and SimPLe [45](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib45). 
*   •Proprio Control This benchmark contains 18 control tasks with continuous actions, proprioceptive vector inputs, and a budget of 500K environment steps [46](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib46). The tasks range from classical control over locomotion to robot manipulation tasks, featuring dense and sparse rewards. Dreamer sets a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming D4PG, DMPO, and MPO [33](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib33). 
*   •Visual Control This benchmark consists of 20 continuous control tasks where the agent receives only high-dimensional images as input and has a budget of 1M environment steps [46](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib46). Dreamer establishes a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming DrQ-v2 and CURL [47](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib47), which are specialized to visual environments and leverage data augmentation. 
*   •BSuite This benchmark includes 23 environments with a total of 468 configurations that are specifically designed to test credit assignment, robustness to reward scale and stochasticity, memory, generalization, and exploration [48](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib48). Dreamer establishes a new state-of-the-art on this benchmark, outperforming Boot DQN and other methods [49](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib49). Dreamer improves over previous algorithms especially in the scale robustness category. 

#### Minecraft

Collecting diamonds in the popular game Minecraft has been a long-standing challenge in artificial intelligence[18](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib18), [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19), [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). Every episode in this game is set in a unique randomly generated and infinite 3D world. Episodes last until the player dies or up to 36000 steps equaling 30 minutes, during which the player needs to discover a sequence of 12 items from sparse rewards by foraging for resources and crafting tools. It takes about 20 minutes for experienced human players to obtain diamonds[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20). We follow the block breaking setting of prior work [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19) because the provided action space would make it challenging for stochastic policies to keep a key pressed for a prolonged time.

Because of the training time in this complex domain, extensive tuning would be difficult for Minecraft. Instead, we apply Dreamer out of the box with its default hyperparameters. As shown in [Figures 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") and[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), Dreamer is the first algorithm to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch without using human data as was required by VPT [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib20) or adaptive curricula[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib19). All the Dreamer agents we trained on Minecraft discover diamonds in 100M environment steps. While several strong baselines progress to advanced items such as the iron pickaxe, none of them discovers a diamond.

#### Ablations

In [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models"), we ablate the robustness techniques and learning signals on a diverse set of 14 tasks to understand their importance. The training curves of individual tasks are included in the supplementary material. We observe that all robustness techniques contribute to performance, most notably the KL objective of the world model, followed by return normalization and symexp twohot regression for reward and value prediction. In general, we find that each individual technique is critical on a subset of tasks but may not affect performance on other tasks.

To investigate the effect of the world model, we ablate the learning signals of Dreamer by stopping either the task-specific reward and value prediction gradients or the task-agnostic reconstruction gradients from shaping its representations. Unlike previous reinforcement learning algorithms that often rely only on task-specific learning signals[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib7), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib8), Dreamer rests predominantly on the unsupervised objective of its world model. This finding could allow for future algorithm variants that leverage pretraining on unsupervised data.

#### Scaling properties

To investigate whether Dreamer can scale robustly, we train 6 model sizes ranging from 12M to 400M parameters, as well as different replay ratios on Crafter [50](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib50) and a DMLab task[43](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib43). The replay ratio affects the number of gradient updates performed by the agent. [Figure 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#Sx2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Robust predictions ‣ Learning algorithm ‣ Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models") shows robust learning with fixed hyperparameters across the compared model sizes and replay ratios. Moreover, increasing the model size directly translates to both higher task performance and a lower data requirement. Increasing the number of gradient steps further reduces the interactions needed to learn successful behaviors. The results show that Dreamer learns robustly across model sizes and replay ratios and that its performance and provides a predictable way for increasing performance given computational resources.

4.1. Offline Diamond Challenge 

We evaluate Dreamer 4 on the Minecraft diamond challenge, a long-horizon control task that re-quires solving several sub tasks, such as gathering materials and crafting tools in a complex proce-durally generated 3D world from raw pixels and mouse and keyboard actions. Human players with Minecraft experience take 20 minutes to collect a diamond on average, corresponding to sequences of 24,000 mouse and keyboard actions. 

Offline setting While previous agents have achieved diamonds in Minecraft through online inter-action with the environment 1,15 , deploying partially-trained policies is often infeasible for practical applications, such as physical robots, because ensuring safety, resetting the scene, and providing rewards in real time is difficult. Instead, we focus on the challenge of learning purely offline from a fixed experience dataset. We only use the VPT contractor dataset 15 —which contains 2.5K hours of videos, actions, and event annotations—without allowing the agent to interact with the environ-ment for learning, and compare to baselines in this offline setting. We follow the VPT evaluation protocol of raw pixel inputs and low-level mouse and keyboard actions, requiring crafting through the in-game user interface. Episodes last 60 minutes, starting from an empty inventory in randomly generated Minecraft worlds. 

Implementation Dreamer 4 learns a single transformer that predicts inputs, actions, rewards, and values. To build a steerable agent, we opt for a multi-task setting and condition the actions, re-wards, and values on task embeddings. We annotate the tasks and their sparse binary rewards using the existing events in the VPT dataset. Table 4 lists the 20 tasks and Table 6 shows the linear prompt sequence that guides the agent to reach diamonds during evaluation in the environment. To amplify the signal in the dataset during behavior cloning, reward modeling, and reinforcement learning, we use data mixture of 50% uniform sequences and 50% relevant sequences that accomplish one of the tasks. The behavioral cloning loss is applied only on the relevant fraction, while the dynamics loss is applied only on the uniform sequences to avoid optimistic generations. We use one-hot task indicators but text embeddings could easily be used. We represent keyboard actions as 23 binary distributions and mouse actions as a categorical with 121 classes using foveated discretization 15 .

4.2. Human Interaction 

To evaluate its ability to predict complex interactions, we train Dreamer 4 on the Minecraft VPT dataset 15 and compare its generations to previous world models on this dataset. For this evaluation, a human player tries to accomplish tasks by playing inside of the world model, as shown in Figure 5. The human player receives the task description and the world model is initialized to a start frame for the task. We select a diverse set of tasks that cover a broad range of object interactions and game mechanics. The tasks include digging a pit, building a wall, chopping a tree, placing and riding a boat, looking away and back at objects, interacting with crafting benches and furnaces, and more. We compare Dreamer 4 to the world models Oasis 46 , Lucid-v1 47 , and MineWorld 48 .Note that we cannot directly compare to Genie 3 7, because it only supports camera actions and one generic “interact” button, whereas Minecraft requires a more general mouse and keyboard action space. 4.3. Action Generalization 

One promise of world models is to leverage diverse unlabeled videos to teach agents about the world. For example, a world model could learn general physics and object interactions from web videos where actions are not available. In this section, we investigate the amount of paired videos with actions that are needed for grounding an embodiment into the Dreamer 4 world model. Intuitively, the world model has to learn a broader distribution of possible outcomes when actions are missing, and can narrow the distribution down when actions are provided. Moreover, we investigate how well the action conditioning generalizes, not just within the same distribution, but also out of distribution to parts of the world specifically held out. To measure the accuracy of the action conditioning, we compare action-conditioned multi-step generations to ground truth videos on the holdout set. We report PSNR and SSIM for 16-step generations given 320 frames of context. 

Amount of actions To understand the amount of video with actions needed to learn action con-ditioning, we train Dreamer 4 on all 2541 hours of videos in the VPT dataset, but only provide actions for a small subset of the videos. When actions are unavailable, the dynamics model is con-ditioned on a learned embedding, as described in Section 3.2. We train Dreamer 4 models with 0, 10, 100, 1000, and 2541 hours of actions. The available actions are the first in sequential order of the dataset, corresponding to fewer unique worlds and players than random shuffling would yield. Figure 7 show the quality of the action conditioning compared to training with no actions at all to training with all actions. With only 10 hours of actions, Dreamer 4 achieves 53% PSNR and 75% SSIM compared to a model trained with all actions. With 100 hours of actions, the performance increases further to 85% PSNR and 100% SSIM. This result demonstrates that world models absorb the majority of their knowledge from unlabeled videos, and require only a small amount of actions. 

Action extrapolation In principle, world models may not only learn action ground from a few actions but also generalize their action conditioning to completely new scenarios. In the future, this could allow world models to absorb general knowledge from diverse web videos to simulate agents in diverse environments. 4.4. Model Design 

World models require high model capacity to predict complex object interactions and fast inference to support imagination training and human interaction for inspection. Moreover, interactive infer-ence prompts different design choices compared to typical video models to enable fast generation of individual frames and prevent accumulating errors. To evaluate each model, we train for 48 hours and then generate 1024 videos of 384 frames (˜ 20 seconds) each without any context, with interactive actions chosen by a fixed behavioral cloning policy. We then split the resulting videos into 16 frame chunks to compute the Frechét Video Distance (FVD) 50 to the holdout dataset.

We then parameterize the model to make x-space predic-tions, compute the loss in x-space, and apply the ramp loss weight. These changes substantially improve generation quality over traditional v-space prediction, especially for long generations. We hypothesize that the prediction tar-gets in x-space are more structured and thus reduce the risk of high-frequency errors that accumulate over time. Using temporal attention only every 4 layers not only speeds up training and inference 39 but also improves generation quality, possibly because of the inductive bias of spatial attention that focuses computation on the current frame. GQA further accelerates generations without degrading performance. Switching the long context layers from dense to time-only attention accelerates inference at a mild quality cost, and prepares us to increase the overall number of tokens subsequently. While the register tokens do not improve FVD measurably, we qualitatively notice that they improve temporal consistency. After these changes, training and inference is fast enough to increase model capacity through more spatial tokens, improving predictions of complex interactions. # 5. Related Work 

Minecraft agents Obtaining diamonds in the video game Minecraft has been a focus of intelligent agent research 51–54 , a long-horizon task that requires gathering resources and crafting tools through thousands of low-level actions in complex procedurally generated 3D worlds. Different setups have been used in the literature, with Table 3 summarizing the ones relevant to our work. VPT 15 collects 2.5K hours of contractor gameplay and uses it to annotate 270K hours of web videos with synthetic mouse and keyboard actions. Behavioral cloning on this large offline dataset and targeted finetuning on “early-game” data yields a policy that occasionally obtains wooden pickaxes. Following up with 194K hours of online reinforcement learning results in a policy that obtains diamonds and diamond pickaxes. Dreamer 3 1 learns to collect diamonds from scratch from 1.4K hours of online interaction, without any human data. It uses the MineRL competition action space that includes abstract crafting actions. Other works have explored novel algorithms for easier tasks 55–58 . In this paper, we train an agent to achieve diamonds purely from the 2.5K hour contractor dataset, without any online interaction. We use low-level mouse and keyboard actions and high-resolution image inputs. 

World model agents Learning behaviors based on learned models of the environment has been explored for a long time 59–61 . Visual Foresight 62 , the work by Ha and Schmidhuber 63 , and PlaNet 64 

achieved world models accurate enough for planning from pixels. With Dreamer, world models have become the state-of-the-art approach for solving control problems with high-dimensional inputs, out-performing model-free reinforcement learning in robustness, efficiency, and final performance 1,65,66 .World models based on transformers or diffusion objectives have demonstrated high data efficiency for discrete control 67–69 . However, these world models have been limited in model capacity, restrict-ing their applicability to relatively simple simulated environments. 

Scalable world models Larger world models have been shown to simulate more complex data distributions 70 . World models like Genie 3 generate highly diverse scenes and simulate camera movement and simple interactions 7,9,10,12 . PlayerOne 8 and PEVA 11 condition on more detailed hu-man movement. Oasis 46 , Lucid 47 , and MineWorld 48 learn Minecraft simulators from mouse and keyboard inputs. Whereas Oasis captures simple game mechanics and achieves real-time inference on specialized hardware, Lucid’s predictions diverge quickly and MineWorld is slower than real time. GameNGen 71 finetunes Stable Diffusion into a playable simulator of a level of the game Doom. DIA-MOND 4 learns a simulator of a level of the game CS GO, achieving short-term predictions. GAIA 72,73 

generates driving scenarios from real world data. However, these world models still struggle to pre-dict complex object interactions precisely enough for imagination training. 

Fast generation Enabling fast and accurate generations has been a long-standing challenge in generating modeling. MaskGit generates discrete tokens in parallel to accelerate sampling over au-toregressive models 74 . Diffusion models are often distilled to enable sampling using fewer forward passes 75,76 , which requires two training phases. Consistency models learn straight paths to en-able fast image generation but require careful schedules 77–79 , with successful applications to video generation 80 . Shortcut models 21 condition flows on both noise level and step size, producing fast generative models in one training phase and without schedules. Mean Flow 81 extends the idea of conditioning on the step size to a continuous time formulation. Efficient and sparse architectures are used for video generation because of the large number of tokens 38,82,83 . These models do not support interactive inference and many of the techniques are complimentary to our work.

# 6. Discussion 

We present Dreamer 4, a scalable agent that learns to solve challenging control tasks by imagination training inside of a fast and accurate world model. Dreamer 4 is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from offline data, without online interaction. This achievement demonstrates its learning successful long-horizon strategies in complex environments. Learning purely from offline datasets enables applications where online interaction is impractical or unsafe. The world model of Dreamer 4 rests on a shortcut forcing objective and an efficient transformer architecture to predict complex object interactions while supporting interactive inference in real time on a single GPU. We demonstrate that it significantly outperforms previous world models on Minecraft, where it accurately predicts a wide range of game mechanics from mouse and keyboard inputs. However, the world model is far from a full clone of the game, especially due to short memory and imprecise inventory predictions, leaving Minecraft as an ideal benchmark for future world model and agent research. We also show that Dreamer 4 learns accurate action conditioning from only a small amount of videos with actions, allowing it to absorb the majority of its knowledge from diverse unlabeled videos. Promising future directions include pretraining on general internet videos, integrating long-term memory into the world model and agent, incorporating language understanding, leveraging small amounts of corrective online data, and automatically discovering goals to break up long tasks. Dreamer 4 offers a reliable and performant starting point for these explorations.

## Inherited decisions

- The frozen LLM remains frozen.
- The current WikiText experiment is strictly causal-prefix prediction:
  \[
  \hat H_{L,t+1:t+K}=f_\theta(H_{M,t-W+1:t})
  \]
  Future tokens, future middle states, and all final states are targets only.
- The deterministic model estimates a conditional mean, not a conditional density.
- The first experiment must retain one training loss, document-level splits, horizon-resolved metrics, shuffled-target controls, and strong pointwise/linear baselines.
- Its valid first claim is narrow: trajectory-conditioned nonlinear prediction of unseen future residuals. It does **not** establish interventions, autonomous rollout, or planning.
- The current aggregate-J runner is a diagnostic, not yet the full per-horizon \(J_\Delta\) experiment.
- Interventions, actions, and planning are excluded from the **first experiment**, not forbidden from the research program.

## Diagnosis

### Evidence ladder

These are four different claims and should never be collapsed:

| Level | Operational evidence | Not yet established |
|---|---|---|
| **Prediction** | A causal prefix predicts held-out future final states better than legal controls | Causality, self-rollout, planning |
| **Causal representation** | Reading identifies a latent intermediate; writing/swapping it causes the frozen LLM to change behavior in the predicted, selective way | Autonomous dynamics or planning |
| **Autonomous rollout** | From one posterior state, the model repeatedly predicts and feeds back its own latent states under actions, without future observations | Choosing useful actions |
| **Planning** | Counterfactual latent rollouts improve realized task return over matched no-planning controls | General planning outside the benchmark |

The Dreamer reports support exactly this separation:

> “Predicting ahead in latent space not only facilitates long-term predictions, it also allows to efficiently predict thousands of compact state sequences in parallel in a single batch, without having to generate images.”

— DreamerV2 report, §2.1, `docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md` (run `eea2fdaf`)

> “The world model learns compact representations of sensory inputs through autoencoding [23] and enables planning by predicting future representations and rewards for potential actions.”

— DreamerV3 report, World model learning, `docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md` (run `5828099b`)

But DreamerV3 also explicitly says:

> “For environment interaction, we select actions by sampling from the actor network without lookahead planning.”

— DreamerV3 report, Critic learning, `docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md` (run `5828099b`)

Thus, imagination-trained control is not automatically online search/planning. For LUCID3’s cleanest first planning proof, use explicit latent lookahead or MPC.

DreamerV4 similarly separates counterfactual simulation from policy improvement:

> “To improve beyond strategies displayed in the dataset, we then finetune the policy through imagination training by reinforcement learning on rollouts generated by the world model, using an additional value head.”

— DreamerV4 report, §3.3, `docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md` (run `f4abcaeb`)

### Concrete findings

| Severity | Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **blocker for rollout/planning claims** | The current predictor is a prefix-to-\(K\)-targets map. It has no recurrent latent transition that consumes its own prediction, no action input, and no reward/termination model. It therefore cannot autonomously roll out or plan. | `docs/pseudocode/conditional_future_residual_predictor.py`; `slop/specs/20260829_conditional_future_residual_predictor.md` |
| **major** | A J-lens-style intervention on the frozen LLM would prove that the intervention direction is causal, but not that LUCID3’s learned compact state is causal unless LUCID3 supplies a read/write path and predicts the intervention effect. | `docs/papers/20260710_global_workspace.md`, §3.1–3.3 |
| **major** | Adding interventions or actions to the first WikiText training graph would conflict with the accepted first-experiment contract and obscure whether ordinary future prediction works. | `AGENTS.md`; `slop/specs/20260829_conditional_future_residual_predictor.md` |
| **major** | A text maze is a reasonable later planning benchmark, but by itself can show only that a small maze model plans. Raw text, explicit coordinates, demonstrations, or the planner itself may solve the task without extracting an LLM latent world model. | Planning assessment below |
| **minor** | A higher classification F1 is not the closest analogue to the J-lens paper’s causal result. The paper reports top-1 swap success and log-probability shifts. Macro-F1 can be secondary on a balanced answer set. | `docs/papers/20260710_global_workspace.md`, Figures 13–15 |

## Drift / contradiction check

The desire to prepare causal and planning demonstrations now is compatible with the inherited plan. The contradiction appears only if they are inserted into the first experiment or presented as conclusions from it.

The quiet assumption that must be rejected is:

> Accurate multi-horizon endpoint prediction implies an autonomous world model.

It does not. The current predictor never transitions from predicted state to predicted state.

A second quiet assumption is:

> Replicating a J-lens coordinate swap proves LUCID3 learned a causal representation.

It proves that the frozen LLM’s edited direction is causal. LUCID3 earns causal-representation language only when its learned compact state can be read, written back, and shown to mediate the expected behavioral change.

## Recommendation: minimal staged evidence program

### Stage 0 — Measurement integrity

Before scientific claims:

- Prove the future-input boundary.
- Preserve official document splits and train-only preprocessing.
- Pass cross-document shuffled-target collapse.
- Lock horizons, stopping, checkpoint selection, seeds, and bootstrap units.
- Complete the current aggregate-J diagnostic seams before fitting full \(J_\Delta\).

**Gate:** no leakage, alignment, provenance, shape, or prefix-invariance failure.

---

### Stage 1 — Unknown-future prediction

**Question:** Does the observed middle-layer trajectory contain nonlinear information about later final states?

#### Mockup: “Prediction without seeing the future”

```text
Observed prefix                                Forbidden future
tokens:  ... the animal that spins webs | is | ...
H_M:     ●──●──●──●──●──●──●──●───────┤  ×   ×   ×
                         │
                     reader/GRU
                         │ z_t
              ┌──────────┼──────────┐
             Δ=2        Δ=4        Δ=8
             Ĥ_L         Ĥ_L         Ĥ_L

Right panel: standardized MSE versus horizon
mean ─────────────
affine-last ───────
nonlinear-last ────
linear-prefix ─────
LUCID3-GRU ─────────  lower is better
```

#### Controls

- Horizon mean.
- Fixed aggregate-J/current basis diagnostic, clearly labeled.
- Fixed-basis last-state and random-basis controls.
- Learned affine-last.
- Decoder-matched nonlinear-last.
- Linear-prefix recurrence.
- Mean-based GRU versus J-based GRU.
- Cross-document shuffled targets.
- Forbidden future-token oracle, diagnostic only.

#### Metrics

- Primary: equally weighted train-standardized MSE over \(\Delta=2\ldots8\).
- Raw MSE, train-mean-centered cosine, and frozen-head teacher-to-prediction KL by horizon.
- Three seeds and paired document-bootstrap intervals.
- Report \(\Delta=1\), but do not let it establish multi-step prediction.

#### Discriminator

- **Trajectory information:** GRU beats nonlinear-last.
- **Nonlinearity:** GRU beats linear-prefix.
- **J-path utility:** J-GRU beats the identical mean-GRU.
- If only MSE improves while frozen-head diagnostics remain poor, that earns a stochastic follow-up—not a planning experiment.
- If no learned model beats the horizon mean, stop and audit rather than proceeding to diffusion or planning.

---

### Stage 2 — Short causal representation proof

This should be the next **separate** experiment after Stage 1’s checkpoint, not another loss in Stage 1.

Start by reproducing the J-lens task on the same frozen Qwen model, then compare LUCID3 against it. Do not compare Qwen numbers directly with proprietary Claude numbers.

The motivating paper’s mockup is unusually strong:

> “When we swap the spider lens vector for ant, the model's top output changes from "8" to "6", the number of legs on an ant.”

— `docs/papers/20260710_global_workspace.md`, §3.3

It also already contains a short planning-like example:

> “When we swap the fight lens vector for light, the model's choice for the next word (before the end of the line) changes from "coming" to "morning," and the overall completion changes from "coming fight" to "morning light."”

— `docs/papers/20260710_global_workspace.md`, §3.3

#### Mockup: “Read, swap, and redirect”

```text
                 CLEAN                         LEARNED-LATENT SWAP
Prompt           animal that spins webs       same prompt
Readout          spider  .72                   spider → ant
Frozen LLM       8  (-0.2)                     6  (-0.1)
LUCID3 predicts  effect toward 8               effect toward 6

                 Actual frozen-LLM rerun       Predicted intervention effect
Residual effect  ───────────────────────────── ●
Logit effect     6 ↑, 8 ↓                      ●

Aggregate panels:
A. target-answer top-1 success
B. target-vs-clean log-odds shift
C. effect error: zero / random / J / LUCID3
D. collateral KL on unrelated outputs
```

#### Required mechanism

1. **Read:** encode a compact state \(z_t\) from the middle-layer prefix.
2. **Edit:** replace the inferred concept/plan coordinate with a held-out alternative.
3. **Write:** decode that edited compact state back into a middle-residual intervention.
4. **Rerun:** let the frozen LLM continue.
5. **Predict:** have LUCID3 predict the resulting future residual/logit effect.

Without step 3, the demonstration is only a visualization of the predictor, not causal evidence.

#### Task families

- Spider \(\rightarrow\) ant, answer 8 \(\rightarrow\) 6.
- Country \(\rightarrow\) capital or object \(\rightarrow\) property.
- Planned rhyme fight \(\rightarrow\) light.
- Repeat \(\leftrightarrow\) switch bandit.
- Held-out templates, concepts, and swap pairs.

#### Controls

- Original J-lens coordinate swap.
- Lag-conditioned/local Jacobian effect predictor.
- Zero-effect baseline.
- Random orthogonal and random-basis edits, norm matched.
- Wrong layer, wrong token position, and sham/no-write edits.
- Direct-answer-vector edit, to rule out smuggling the answer.
- Non-J-space or residual complement edit.
- Clean accuracy and intervention specificity.
- Predeclared strengths; no choosing the best test-time strength after seeing answers.

#### Metrics

- Top-1 target-answer swap success with Wilson or paired bootstrap intervals.
- Target-versus-clean-answer log-odds shift.
- Macro-F1 across balanced answer labels as a secondary summary.
- Residual- and logit-space intervention effect error.
- Collateral KL and unrelated-task accuracy.
- Effect error must beat the zero-effect baseline with uncertainty; fixed-future edits remain exploratory otherwise.
- Cluster uncertainty by prompt/template and concept pair.

**Gate:** learned read/write edits outperform zero and random controls, match actual frozen-model effects, and cause selective target-consistent behavior without direct-answer leakage.

This is the most valuable near-term figure. It is cheaper and more aligned with LUCID3 than starting with a maze.

---

### Stage 3 — Autonomous action-conditioned rollout

Prediction of \(K\) endpoints is not enough. Introduce a distinct transition experiment:

\[
z_t=q(H_{M,\le t}),\qquad
\hat z_{t+1}\sim p_\phi(z_{t+1}\mid z_t,a_t).
\]

The rollout must self-feed:

\[
\hat z_{t+2}\sim p_\phi(z_{t+2}\mid \hat z_{t+1},a_{t+1}),
\]

with no future token, observation, residual, or posterior correction.

A text environment requires a new episodic dataset; WikiText has neither explicit actions nor rewards. This is an intentional later revision of the WikiText-only setting, not a change to Stage 1.

#### Mockup: “Teacher-forced versus imagined”

```text
Ground truth:       z0 --N--> z1 --E--> z2 --E--> z3 --S--> goal
One-step posterior: z0 --N--> ẑ1    reset   ẑ2    reset   ẑ3
Autonomous rollout: z0 --N--> ẑ1 --E--> ẑ2 --E--> ẑ3 --S--> reward

Panels:
- latent/state error versus rollout horizon
- reward and termination calibration
- action sensitivity: correct / shuffled / no-action
- decoded location-belief maps
```

#### Controls

- Posterior-reset one-step prediction versus fully autonomous rollout.
- Last residual only.
- Raw text/token embedding dynamics.
- Linear latent dynamics.
- No-action and shuffled-action dynamics.
- Shuffled next-state targets.
- Oracle symbolic-state transition.
- Memory ablation for aliased observations.

#### Metrics

- Latent prediction error to held-out posterior states.
- Symbolic state/location probe accuracy, diagnostic only.
- Reward and termination AUROC/Brier score.
- Action-conditioned counterfactual accuracy.
- Compounding error and valid-rollout rate by horizon.
- Multi-step calibration on held-out layouts.

**Gate:** action changes predicted futures correctly, and autonomous rollouts remain informative over the horizons needed for the planning task.

---

### Stage 4 — Planning in a procedural text maze

A maze is appropriate **here**, but only with safeguards.

#### Recommended maze design

- Procedurally generated layouts split by generator seed.
- Local, partially observed textual descriptions; no absolute coordinates or full-map dump.
- Actions such as north/east/south/west.
- Collisions, sparse goal reward, and explicit termination.
- Exploratory offline trajectories, not only shortest-path demonstrations.
- Held-out layouts and path lengths, e.g. 5–40 decisions.
- Frozen LLM supplies residual trajectories; the compact reader and dynamics remain the evaluated object.

Use online latent beam search or MPC for the first planning proof. That gives a direct operational meaning to “planning,” unlike an actor that executes without lookahead.

#### Mockup: “Imagine alternatives, then act”

```text
Current observation / latent belief
                 z_t
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
     N,E,E       E,N,N       S,S,E
      z...         z...       z...
   R̂ = 0.82     R̂ = 0.10   R̂ = 0.03
       │
 choose first N, execute in real maze, re-encode, replan

Right panels:
- environment success versus shortest-path length
- success versus search budget
- SPL / regret
- planning enabled / no-lookahead / shuffled dynamics / oracle
```

#### Planning controls

- Random and greedy/no-lookahead policies.
- Same policy or action scorer without imagined rollouts.
- Behavior cloning from the same data.
- Raw-text and last-residual world models under the **same planner**.
- Linear dynamics under the same planner.
- Shuffled-action, shuffled-transition, and horizon-one ablations.
- Oracle symbolic-state planner as upper bound.
- Frozen LLM direct-action baseline.
- Search-budget sweep.

#### Metrics

- Real-environment success rate.
- Success weighted by path length, excess steps, and regret to shortest path.
- Success by required planning depth and observation aliasing.
- Correlation/calibration between predicted and realized candidate-sequence returns.
- Planning gain over the same no-lookahead policy.
- Compute-normalized success.

#### Decisive planning result

Planning is supported only if:

1. latent lookahead improves actual-environment success over the matched no-lookahead policy;
2. gains increase with useful search depth or budget;
3. shuffled-action/dynamics or horizon-one ablations remove the gain;
4. raw text, last-state, and linear controls do not match it;
5. performance generalizes to held-out layouts and longer paths.

If the raw-text planner matches LUCID3, the maze was solved, but compact LLM-latent planning was not demonstrated.

## Maze versus J-lens replication

| Choice | Strength | Main limitation | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Replicate J-lens figures** | Cheap, legible, causally grounded in the frozen LLM, directly connected to residual coordinates | Does not establish self-rollout or external task planning | **Do first after prediction** |
| **Text maze** | Supplies explicit actions, counterfactual branches, rewards, and exact realized outcomes | Strong shortcut risk; requires a new dataset and a genuinely autonomous transition model | **Do after action-conditioned rollout passes** |

They are complements, not alternatives. The strongest minimal paper arc is:

1. future residual prediction;
2. learned causal read/write intervention;
3. autonomous action-conditioned latent rollout;
4. maze planning with disabling ablations.

## Risks

- Deterministic future residuals may average incompatible token continuations.
- A concept swap may inherit causality entirely from the J basis rather than the learned compact state.
- A learned writer may directly encode expected answers instead of an intermediate concept.
- Fixed-future intervention tests may fail to transfer to free generation.
- Final-layer residuals may be prediction targets but poor recurrent states; autonomous dynamics may require a separate compact posterior state.
- Maze observations may reveal too much state, allowing direct reactive control.
- Offline maze coverage may be insufficient for counterfactual action evaluation.
- Search may exploit model errors; predicted return must be checked against realized return.
- Dreamer-style imagination training is control through imagined experience, but not necessarily test-time lookahead planning.

## Need from main agent

No blocking decision is required. Preserve Stage 1 unchanged, but prepare Stage 2’s prompt library and intervention protocol now. Execute it as a separate gated experiment after a predictive checkpoint exists.

## Suggested execution prompt

No executor handoff is warranted for this advisory task.

85:(1) All components are implemented as neural networks and φ describes their combined parameter vector. The transition predictor guesses the next model state only from the current model state and the action but without using the next image, so that we can later learn behaviors by predicting sequences of model states without having to observe or generate images. The discount predictor lets us estimate the probability of an episode ending when learning behaviors from model predictions. 
129:DreamerV2 learns long-horizon behaviors purely within its world model using an actor and a critic. The actor chooses actions for predicting imagined sequences of compact model states. The critic accumulates the future predicted rewards to take into account rewards beyond the planning horizon. Both the actor and critic operate on top of the learned model states and thus benefit from the representations learned by the world model. The world model is fixed during behavior learning, so the actor and value gradients do not affect its representations. Not predicting images during behavior learning lets us efficiently simulate 2500 latent trajectories in parallel on a single GPU. 
153:. (3) In contrast to the actual environment, the latent state sequence is Markovian, so that there is no need for the actor and critic to condition on more than the current model state. The actor and critic are both MLPs with ELU activations (Clevert et al., 2015) and use 1M trainable parameters each. The actor outputs a categorical distribution over actions and the critic has a deterministic output. The two components are trained from the same imagined trajectories but optimize separate loss functions. 
96:Figure 4: Multi-step video predictions of a DMLab maze (top) and a quadrupedal robot (bottom). Given 5 context images and the full action sequence, the model predicts 45 frames into the future without access to intermediate images. The world model learns an understanding of the underlying structure of each environment.
116:The actor and critic neural networks learn behaviors purely from abstract trajectories of representations predicted by the world model [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib14). For environment interaction, we select actions by sampling from the actor network without lookahead planning. The actor and critic operate on model states s_{t}\doteq\{h_{t},z_{t}\} and thus benefit from the Markovian representations learned by the recurrent world model. The actor aims to maximize the return R_{t}\doteq\textstyle\sum_{\tau=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau}r_{t+\tau} with a discount factor \gamma=0.997 for each model state. To consider rewards beyond the prediction horizon T=16, the critic learns to approximate the distribution of returns [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib28) for each state under the current actor behavior:
98:The prediction loss trains the decoder and reward predictor via the symlog squared loss described later, and the continue predictor via logistic regression. The dynamics loss trains the sequence model to predict the next representation by minimizing the KL divergence between the predictor p_{\phi}(z_{t}\;|\;h_{t}) and the next stochastic representation q_{\phi}(z_{t}\;|\;h_{t},x_{t}). The representation loss, in turn, trains the representations to become more predictable allowing us to use a factorized dynamics predictor for fast sampling during imagination training. The two losses differ in the stop-gradient operator \operatorname{sg}(\cdot) and their loss scale. To avoid a degenerate solution where the dynamics are trivial to predict but fail to contain enough information about the inputs, we employ free bits[26](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.04104v2#bib.bib26) by clipping the dynamics and representation losses below the value of 1 nat \approx 1.44 bits. This disables them while they are already minimized well to focus learning on the prediction loss:
159:(6) Shortcut models parameterize the network to predict velocities 𝑣 = 𝑥 1 − 𝑥 0, called v-prediction 26 .This approach excels when generating the output jointly as one block, such as for image or video generation models. However, v-prediction trains the network to produce high-frequency outputs. When iteratively generating long videos frame by frame, this can cause subtle errors that accumulate over time. Instead, we found that parameterizing the network to predict clean representations, called x-prediction, enables high-quality rollouts of arbitrary length. Computing the flow loss term in x-space is straightforward 26 . To compute the bootstrap loss term, we convert the network output into v-space and scale the resulting loss back into x-space ∗:
193:To solve control tasks, we first adapt the pretrained world model to predict actions and rewards from the dataset conditioned on one of multiple tasks. For this, we insert agent tokens as an additional modality into the world model transformer and interleave it with the image representations, actions, and register tokens. The agent tokens receive task embeddings as input and we use them to predict the policy and reward model using MLP heads. While the agent tokens attend to themselves and all other modalities, no other modalities can attend back to the agent tokens. This is crucial for avoiding causal confusion of the world model—its future predictions can only be directly influenced                      
311:Agent performance Figure 3 compares the agent performance on the diamond task. We re-port the success rates for several relevant items leading up to diamonds that are listed in Table 5. VPT (finetuned) progresses up to sticks, which it achieves 53% of the time. It also collects a small amount of stone, iron ore, and iron ingots through edge cases, such as exploding Creeper mobs and loot chests. Using the contractor actions directly instead of annotating YouTube videos, our modern BC baseline achieves higher performance than VPT (finetuned). VLA (Gemma 3) shows that ini-tializing the policy from a pretrained models offers significant benefits, progressing up to the iron pickaxe with a success rate of 11%. Dreamer 4 achieves high success rates of over 90% up to the stone pickaxe, a success rate of 29% for the iron pickaxe, and obtains diamonds in 0.7% of episodes. Imagination training shows stronger improvements over the behavior cloning agents the more chal-lenging the milestone is. Figure 4 compares additional agents on the diamond task, showing that the world model representations outperform the general representations of Gemma 3 for behavioral cloning. This indicates that video prediction implicitly learns an understanding of the world that is also useful for decision making. Finally, imagination training consistently improves not only the success rates but also makes the policy more efficient so that it reaches the milestones faster. 
96:Figure 4: Multi-step video predictions of a DMLab maze (top) and a quadrupedal robot (bottom). Given 5 context images and the full action sequence, the model predicts 45 frames into the future without access to intermediate images. The world model learns an understanding of the underlying structure of each environment.

content.text:
You’re right to reject the earlier answer. I read the methods, experiments, and ablations across DreamerV2–V4, plus the successful and failed maze work in LUCID2.

## One goal, two proofs

I think `AGENTS.md` should say:

> Goal: extract a compact, nonlinear latent dynamics model from a frozen language model that can be used for planning.

Then prove that one goal with two demonstrations:

1. Short causal demonstration: the latent state is load-bearing and selectively editable.
2. Long-horizon planning demonstration: counterfactual latent rollouts improve decisions, and disabling the dynamics removes that improvement.

The autonomous-agent instruction should move under working rules. It is not one of the scientific goal’s “parts.”

## What Dreamer actually contributes

### DreamerV2: a dynamics state must advance without the next observation

> “The transition predictor guesses the next model state only from the current model state and the action but without using the next image, so that we can later learn behaviors by predicting sequences of model states without having to observe or generate images.”

— [`docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md:85`](docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md)

It then freezes the world model during behavior learning:

> “The actor chooses actions for predicting imagined sequences of compact model states. [...] The world model is fixed during behavior learning.”

— [`docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md:129`](docs/papers/2020_dreamerv2.md)

This gives us an important discriminator: LUCID3 has a latent dynamics model only when a predicted state can be fed back into the transition under an action. Predicting eight future endpoints from one observed prefix is useful, but it is not yet autonomous dynamics.

### DreamerV3: multi-step prediction is action-conditioned and observation-free

> “Given 5 context images and the full action sequence, the model predicts 45 frames into the future without access to intermediate images.”

— [`docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:96`](docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md)

V3 also trains representations to be predictable:

> “The representation loss, in turn, trains the representations to become more predictable allowing us to use a factorized dynamics predictor for fast sampling during imagination training.”

— [`docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:98`](docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md)

However, DreamerV3’s deployed actor does not perform test-time search:

> “For environment interaction, we select actions by sampling from the actor network without lookahead planning.”

— [`docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md:116`](docs/papers/2023_dreamerv3.md)

So “Dreamer planning” often means learning a policy from imagined trajectories, not necessarily searching candidate plans during deployment. For a simple LUCID3 proof, explicit latent beam search or model-predictive control would be easier to interpret.

### DreamerV4: the strongest controls are causal action-following and disabled imagination

V4 isolates task information from world dynamics:

> “This is crucial for avoiding causal confusion of the world model—its future predictions can only be directly influenced by actions, not by the current task.”

— [`docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:193`](docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md)

It also compares behavior cloning with the same model before and after imagination training. The improvements grow on harder milestones:

> “Imagination training shows stronger improvements over the behavior cloning agents the more challenging the milestone is.”

— [`docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md:311`](docs/papers/2025_dreamer4.md)

That is the pattern we want: same model and data, planning enabled versus disabled, with a larger difference as required horizon increases.

## Proof 1: reproduce and extend the J-lens causal figures

Yes, I recommend doing this. It is not planning, but it tests whether the learned latent is causally load-bearing.

```text
Prompt: “The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is”

                         clean z       spider→ant edit     placebo
latent concept            spider            ant             spider
LUCID3 prediction            8               6                8
actual frozen-Qwen output     8               6                8
```

Across held-out concepts and templates, show:

| Measurement | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Target-answer swap success or balanced macro-F1 | Does the behavioral answer follow the intended edit? |
| Target-versus-original log-odds change | Detects partial effects hidden by top-1 accuracy |
| Predicted versus actual residual/logit effect error | Tests whether LUCID3 predicts the intervention, not only causes something |
| Unrelated-output KL or accuracy | Detects broad destructive edits |
| Zero, random, wrong-position, and off-target edits | Tests selectivity |
| Original J-lens versus learned LUCID3 edit | Tests whether nonlinear conditioning improves on the linear baseline |

Higher F1 than the J-lens would be useful, but F1 alone is insufficient. A destructive edit can change answers while having poor effect fidelity and large collateral damage.

I would reproduce several Anthropic-style families on the same frozen Qwen:

- spider → ant: 8 → 6;
- inferred object → different property;
- fight → light: completion changes toward the new rhyme;
- hidden intermediate concepts in two-step questions.

This gives a legible first figure.

## Proof 2: stronger text-maze planning

The LUCID2 maze is worth reusing as a visual language, but not as the final proof standard. Its accepted result was explicitly narrow:

> “observed-edge memory-conditioned planning,” with `k<=3` and two-step plan selection.

It stored learned source and destination fields plus an exact action field, then restricted retrieval to matching actions. That proved structured traversal, but not autonomous prediction of unknown transitions.

A stronger LUCID3 version:

```text
Observed maze history ──Read──> z₀
```
